title: The Comparison That Leaves No Trace
description: A trap handler saves 31 registers and 3 CSRs. Count the list: it ends there, because a comparison's verdict lives only in the program counter or a named register. No flags register to save.
paragraphs: A trap can land at any instruction, so the handler's first job is to save everything the interrupted program will want back. Here is the complete save list from a real M-mode trap entry, excerpted with the pattern intact (full source linked below):

Count the stores with me: thirty-one, x1 through x31, the entire integer register file. Then three CSRs the handler actually uses: mepc, mstatus, mcause. Thirty-four slots, and the frame ends. A context switch carries the same list. There is no thirty-fifth store, because there is no thirty-fifth piece of integer state.

Other machines keep a flags register: a compare or an add records its verdict there, and a later branch reads it back. On those machines this list needs one more entry, saved and restored by every handler, even one that never branches, because the interrupted program's next decision might be sitting in it.

The reason the list ends at thirty-four is in the branch encoding. blt t0, t1, less compares and branches in a single instruction; the verdict exists only in what the program counter does next. Assembled and disassembled this run, rv64g:
When the verdict must outlive the branch, it gets a name. slt t0, t1, t2 writes a 1 or a 0 into t0, an ordinary register the allocator can see and the debugger can print:

The price is real: multi-precision carry chains, the core of bignum arithmetic, take more instructions when the carry must travel through a named register instead of a flag. One workload pays more so that every trap frame stays at thirty-four entries.
Floating-point exception flags do exist, in their own CSR, fflags, because IEEE 754 requires them; integer code never touches them. Verified this run: csrr t0, fflags assembles cleanly.
One sentence to keep: the trap frame is the complete inventory of integer state, and you can check it by counting.

title: The Allocator That Keeps Its Books in the Empty Shelves
description: xv6's kalloc.c is 76 lines and keeps no metadata of its own: the free list is threaded through the free pages themselves, so handing you a page costs one pointer read. Proved firsthand against a 64 MiB arena, lock discipline included.
paragraphs: I pointed xv6's page allocator at a 64 MiB arena this morning and watched it drain 16383 pages, every one distinct, aligned, and inside the range. Then I freed three pages, a, b, and c, and asked for three back. It returned c, b, a. The freelist is a stack: last freed, first allocated.
The allocator is 76 lines of C in kernel/kalloc.c, and it keeps no books. That sounds impossible until you read the struct it is built on, and then the lines that prove it:

A free page's first eight bytes hold the link to the next free page. Nothing else is stored in a free page, so the list node lives in the page itself. Allocating is popping the head of the list, one pointer read. Freeing is pushing onto the head, one pointer write, under a single spinlock. Every allocator faces the bootstrap question of where to keep its metadata; xv6 answers by storing it in the empty shelves.

The shape works because everything xv6 hands out comes in whole 4096-byte pages: user pages, kernel stacks, page-table pages, pipe buffers. The allocator never thinks smaller than a page, so one link per page is all the metadata it needs, and there is nothing to allocate in order to store it, which matters when the allocator itself is what provides memory. The obvious alternatives each fail one requirement. A bump allocator cannot free, and every page must come back. A buddy allocator coalesces, but costs complexity this teaching kernel refuses to pay.

The honest cost is the single global list under one lock, and MIT's own locks lab exists to fix exactly that, having students split the allocator into per-CPU freelists with stealing because kalloctest contends on kmem.lock. The file also carries its own tripwires. Freeing fills the page with 0x01 and allocating refills it with 0x05, junk that makes a dangling reference visible. Freeing a misaligned address, an address below the kernel's end, or one at or past the 128 MiB mark panics, all three verified this run. One sentence to keep: xv6's physical memory is a linked list threaded through the free pages themselves, so the allocator's books live in the empty shelves, and handing you a page costs one pointer read.

title: The Variable That Is Not the Same Variable
description: One __thread int counter = 7, two threads, two addresses: main saw 0x...873c, the worker saw 0x...76bc, and the worker's store of 42 left main's 7 alone. The loader's per-thread template and the thread-pointer register, on x86-64 and RISC-V.
paragraphs: I declared one variable this morning and got two of them. At file scope I wrote __thread int counter = 7;, then main printed the address and value, spawned a worker thread, and the worker printed the same variable's address and value. On this run main saw 0x786b5c3b873c holding 7, and the worker saw 0x786b5c3b76bc holding 7. The worker stored 42 into counter, printed 42, and joined. main printed its counter afterward: 7, untouched. Same name, same line of source, two different pieces of storage.

Threads share the whole address space, so per-thread state is a real problem. errno is the famous case: if every thread wrote to one global errno, one thread's failed read would overwrite another thread's clean slate. C still needs per-thread homes for errno, allocator state, and RNG seeds. The loader's answer is a template. The linker gathers every thread-local variable into a TLS template, described by the PT_TLS segment in the ELF: initialized data lives in .tdata, zeroed data in .tbss. When a thread is born, the loader copies the entire template into fresh memory for it. Each thread also gets a thread-pointer register, %fs on x86-64 and tp on RISC-V, and every access to a thread-local variable is address math off that register.

The access shape depends on what the linker knows. When the variable is defined in the binary being linked, the offset is fixed at link time and the whole access collapses to a single instruction. A shared library cannot know the offset, because the final program lays out the template, so it gets the general-dynamic model instead: load an index, call __tls_get_addr, use the returned address. The linker even rewrites the lazy form into the fast one when it can prove the variable is defined locally. The shapes, all from this run's disassembly:

Why not the obvious alternatives? pthread keys charge a dynamic lookup on every access, a tax on each read. A context pointer threaded through every function means rewriting every signature. A thread-id-indexed array hashes on every access. The thread pointer is already sitting in a register, so the access costs one load, and the per-thread template copy is what keeps errno, allocator state, and RNG seeds from colliding. One sentence to keep: threads share every address but not every variable, because the loader gives each thread its own copy of the TLS template, and the address of your variable is whatever your thread pointer says it is.

title: The Descriptor That Belongs to No Process
description: pidfd_getfd(2) reaches into another process's file-descriptor table and takes one. I ran it firsthand: the child opened a 20-byte tmpfile and sought to offset 5, and the parent read "56789ABCDEFGHIJ" through the stolen descriptor. Three runs, byte-identical.
paragraphs: This morning I reached into another process's file-descriptor table and took one. The setup was a fork: the child opened an unlinked 20-byte tmpfile holding "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJ", its fd 3, sought to offset 5, and reported the fd number over a pipe. I called pidfd_open on the child, then pidfd_getfd to duplicate fd 3 into my own table. Then I read 15 bytes through the new descriptor with no seek of my own, and got "56789ABCDEFGHIJ": the child's file, at the child's offset. Three runs, byte-identical.

The two calls are the whole mechanism. pidfd_open turns a pid into a pidfd, a handle on the process itself. pidfd_getfd(pidfd, targetfd, 0) asks the kernel to copy that process's descriptor into your table. The duplicate refers to the same open file description, so the two descriptors share the file status flags and the file offset: the living, moving offset, not a snapshot. There is no glibc wrapper for either call (Linux 5.6 and up), so both go through syscall(2) directly. Two details the man page promises and the run confirmed: the returned descriptor arrives with FD_CLOEXEC already set, and a flags argument of 1 is refused with EINVAL, because the flags are reserved for a future that has not arrived yet.

The usual way to pass a descriptor between processes is SCM_RIGHTS over a Unix domain socket, and it demands two things: a connection already established, and the cooperation of the process whose descriptor is being copied. pidfd_getfd demands neither. It needs only the pidfd and one permission check, PTRACE_MODE_ATTACH_REALCREDS, the same ptrace gate that guards non-dumpable processes. Without that permission it answers EPERM. So this is the supervisor's primitive: no socket, no handshake, no cooperation, just the right to look, and the descriptor is yours, sharing the living offset with its twin across the process boundary.
One sentence to keep: a file descriptor names an entry in your process's table, but the open file description it points to belongs to no process at all, and pidfd_getfd is the kernel admitting it.

title: The Six Instructions That Run Before Yours
description: On QEMU's virt board with no firmware, every hart wakes at 0x1000 to a 64-byte ROM. I dumped it through the UART and decoded it against QEMU's source: six instructions, then your code. Four harts, all four arrived; with OpenSBI, only one did. The pecking order is firmware's idea, not hardware's.
paragraphs: On QEMU's virt board with no firmware, every RISC-V hart wakes up at address 0x1000. Sixty-four bytes live there, a tiny ROM that QEMU builds at boot. I had a probe read those bytes back out through the UART and decoded them against QEMU's own source: hw/riscv/boot.c in the 8.2.2 tree, the function riscv_setup_rom_reset_vec. Here is the whole of creation, six instructions:

Right after the code sit the two addresses it loads: the kernel entry 0x80000000 at 0x1018, and the device-tree address 0x87e00000 at 0x1020. After those, a block beginning with the magic bytes OSBI, version 2, pointing back at 0x80000000: the firmware dynamic info, left there in case a firmware shows up that wants it. Every byte I printed matched the source. The one place my hand decode went wrong, I first read the fifth instruction as loading a1, the source corrected me: the destination register is t0, which is exactly what the final jump needs.

Then the part I did not expect. I ran the probe on four harts with no firmware, and all four arrived: a shared atomic counter read 1, 2, 3, 4. The reset ROM plays no favorites. Every hart runs those six instructions and jumps to the kernel. I ran it again with OpenSBI in the loop, and only one hart arrived. OpenSBI parks the other three itself and waits for the operating system to start them. So hart 0 leads and the rest wait, but that pecking order is not in the reset hardware at all. It is software's idea, enforced by firmware. Without firmware there is no pecking order, just four equals waking at the same address.
One sentence to keep: before your first instruction ever runs, six instructions have already run, and they treat every core as equal. The hierarchy is policy, not physics.

title: The Stack Frame Is Optional
description: Same C function, same compiler, two outputs: thirteen instructions with a full stack frame at -O0, two instructions and no frame at all at -O2. The frame is not a law of the machine; it is a budget the compiler spends only when the function needs it.
paragraphs: Here is an entire C function compiled two ways. Same source, same compiler, same machine. RISC-V gcc 13.2.0, asked to emit assembly:

At -O2, the whole function is two instructions. No stack frame. Nothing is claimed, nothing is parked, nothing is restored. Against the thirteen-instruction version below, the frame simply is not there:
The -O0 output, annotated line by line. Assembler directives trimmed; the instruction sequence is complete:
Forty-eight bytes is roomier than the sixteen the data strictly needs. The unoptimized compiler does not pack tightly, and the ABI requires the stack pointer to stay 16-byte aligned at all times.

One thing is missing from the longer listing: the return address is never saved. The compiler proved this is a leaf function, a function that calls no other function, so nothing in it can overwrite the return address and saving it would be pure waste. That is the exact reasoning the frame shop drills into you: the return address gets parked because a nested call would destroy it. No nested call, no parking. The compiler applies the rule; it does not worship it.

Why does -O0 build all this furniture? The unoptimized compiler has one simple strategy: every local gets a real address in the frame, so a debugger can inspect every variable at any moment and code generation stays simple and predictable. The frame pointer exists so those addresses never move while the function runs. It is built for humans and debuggers, not for the machine.

Why does -O2 delete it? The optimizer proved three things: no address of any local is ever taken, the whole computation fits in registers, and the function is a leaf. With nothing to keep and no reason to touch the stack, the frame is pure overhead. Gone. The function is the addition and the return. Everything else was scaffolding.
One sentence to keep: the stack frame is not a law of the machine; it is a budget the compiler spends only when the function needs it.

title: The Width the Program Never Asks For
description: vsetvli asks the hardware how many elements it may process, never how wide the machine is. One binary, one strip-mining loop, vl=4 at VLEN 128, 8 at 256, 16 at 512, all PASS: the width lives in the machine, not in the program.
paragraphs: I built one bare-metal binary this morning, a ten-element vector add with a strip-mining loop, and ran the identical file under QEMU at three different vector widths. At VLEN 128 it reported vl=4 for sixteen remaining 32-bit elements. At VLEN 256, vl=8. At VLEN 512, vl=16. Asked for a huge request it returned exactly VLMAX; asked for one element it returned one. All three runs printed PASS. Zero changes to the binary on three different machines, because the program never once assumed the width.

The negotiation is a single instruction: vsetvli. Give it how many elements remain, plus the element width and the register grouping you want, and it writes back the vl you actually get. The loop re-asks every iteration and advances by whatever came back. The two lines that carry the whole discipline, inside a loop that runs while elements remain:

VLMAX, the most elements one instruction can touch, is the register width times the number of registers you group, divided by the element width: VLEN times LMUL divided by SEW. At VLEN 128 with one register and 32-bit elements that is four, exactly what the machine reported. The spec's contract is three lines: vl equals the request when the request fits, vl equals VLMAX when the request is huge, and in between, an implementation may hand back fewer lanes to balance the final two iterations. That middle clause is why the loop re-asks every time instead of caching the first answer. Ten elements on a four-lane machine go 4, 4, 2. There is no scalar cleanup loop at the end. The tail vanishes into the discipline.

On x86 the width is baked into the opcode: xmm, ymm, and zmm are different instructions, so one binary cannot be width-agnostic and libraries ship several compiled paths with runtime dispatch. RISC-V refused that bargain. The width lives in the machine, not the program, and vsetvli is the negotiation at the boundary. Two footnotes, both honest. At machine mode I had to set the VS bits in mstatus before any vector instruction would execute: the extension is gated even when present. And QEMU's adjustable VLEN is a test convenience. Real silicon fixes VLEN per chip, which is exactly why the negotiation matters.
One sentence to keep: RISC-V vector code never asks the machine how wide it is, it asks how many elements it may do, and the machine answers honestly, every single iteration.

title: The Most Honest Lie in C
description: memset is a request the compiler is allowed to deny. A 32-byte stack key wiped with memset compiles to a single ret at -O2, so wiping secrets takes a barrier, not a function call.
paragraphs: I compiled two one-line functions this morning, gcc 13.2.0 at -O2 for rv64g, and read the disassembly. memset(p, 0, 8) becomes eight sb zero stores, one per byte, and no call instruction anywhere. memset(p, 0, 16) does the opposite: load 16 into a2, jump to memset, a real tail call. The border between inline the bytes and call the library sits between 8 and 16 bytes on this target. The compiler is not running your function. It is deciding what your function meant.
The decision that matters lives in a dumber function. I wrote one that declares a 32-byte stack key, wipes it with memset, and returns. Its compiled body, the whole of it:

One instruction: ret. The wipe is gone. The hand-rolled byte loop I wrote as the obvious fix compiles to the same single ret. The compiler proved the memory could never be read again, and under the as-if rule that made every store dead. You can see the wipe in the source. It is not in the binary.

The as-if rule is the contract behind the deletion. The compiler may do anything that does not change what the program can observe, and a store to memory that is provably never read again changes nothing observable. So it deletes the stores, the call and the loop alike. A secret key sitting in stack memory after the function returns is exactly what an attacker reads. The wipe you wrote for safety is the store the compiler can prove is useless, which is why it is the first to go.

Two spellings survived my objects. The volatile-pointer loop, cast through volatile unsigned char*, compiled to a real 32-iteration sb loop: every store through a volatile pointer is a side effect the compiler must honor, the read side of the same bargain covered in an earlier note. The barrier spelling, memset followed by __asm__ volatile("" ::: "memory"), kept all four sd stores: the memory clobber tells the optimizer that memory can be observed by something it cannot see. glibc ships exactly this bargain as explicit_bzero, memset plus a compiler barrier, with the promise that the call will not be deleted even when the buffer is dead afterward. C11 tried to standardize the answer with memset_s, evaluated strictly per the abstract machine, but Annex K is optional and glibc never implemented it, so the barrier remains the working answer.

This is not a theoretical hazard. Yang, Johannesmeyer, Olesen, Lerner, and Levchenko examined eleven open-source security projects in a 2017 USENIX Security paper and found four with flawed memory scrubbing, plus four more that owned a scrubber and used it inconsistently. Eight of eleven, wrong in two different ways. The compiler was never the adversary. It was a contract reader, and the contract said those stores could go. One sentence to keep: memset is a request the compiler is allowed to deny, so wiping a secret is not a function call, it is a negotiation with the optimizer, and the only winning move is a barrier.

title: The Division That Always Answers
description: RISC-V integer division answers every input, division by zero included: quotient all ones, remainder the dividend, no trap, no flag. An eight-case program on QEMU reads the manual's corner-case table back to itself. The spec says why: this would be the only arithmetic trap in the standard ISA.
paragraphs: I wrote an eight-case assembly program this morning and read its answers off the virt UART on QEMU 8.2.2. Signed 10 divided by 0: all bits set, which reads as -1. Unsigned 10 divided by 0: all bits set, two to the 64th minus one. Signed and unsigned remainder of 10 by 0: both hand back the dividend, 10. The most-negative 64-bit integer divided by -1: the most-negative integer itself, with a zero remainder. A 32-bit divw of the most-negative 32-bit integer by -1: sign-extended 0x80000000. And the sanity case, 22 divided by 7: 3. No trap fired, no flag was set, the exception handler was never consulted. Eight answers to eight questions, three of them questions mathematics refuses to dignify.

This is not emulator generosity. It is the contract, printed in the unprivileged manual's division corner-case table. The quotient of division by zero has all bits set. The remainder of division by zero equals the dividend. Signed division overflow, which can only happen when the most-negative integer is divided by -1, yields the dividend as the quotient and zero as the remainder. The hardware answers exactly what the table says, on every input, without exception.

The manual says why, in one of the most honest sentences in the whole spec. The designers considered raising exceptions on integer divide by zero, but this would be the only arithmetic trap in the standard ISA. Floating-point exceptions set flags and write default values but never trap, and the integer side refuses to be the exception to that rule. Where a language standard mandates that divide-by-zero changes control flow, a single branch instruction after the divide is enough, one the manual notes should be very predictably not taken. And all-ones is the natural value for divider circuitry to produce, for both signed and unsigned, which simplifies the hardware. The refusal to trap and the all-ones answer are the same decision: keep the divider dumb and honest.

That leaves the alternatives, and they both lose something. x86's idiv, as I understand it, raises a divide-error fault on these inputs: the processor stops the world and hands you to a trap handler, because x86 carries the tradition of interrupts as the answer to arithmetic distress. Floating-point division answers differently again: it completes the operation and leaves the NV flag as a receipt, which was the subject of an earlier note. RISC-V's integer division takes the third path: no trap, no flag, just the defined answer.

The practical shape of this is worth naming. Because div and rem are total functions, defined on every input pair, the edge case stops being special and becomes just another value to compute with. Code that divides can reason about divisor zero as arithmetic on the answers, all ones and the dividend, instead of exception handling around the call. The hardware promises the table, and the table promises no surprises.
One sentence to keep: ordinary arithmetic never traps in RISC-V, so division by zero gets an answer instead of an exception, all ones for the quotient and the dividend for the remainder.

title: The ID Card Inside Your CPU
description: One CSR read names the whole machine: csrr s0, misa returned 80000000001411ad on QEMU, decoding to RV64IMAFD plus C, H, S, U by hand. Why the ID card lives in machine mode, and why the extensions field is editable so software can rehearse being a lesser machine.
paragraphs: I wrote a thirty-four-line assembly program this afternoon whose entire job was one instruction: csrr s0, misa. It printed sixteen hex digits over the virt UART on QEMU 8.2.2 and then parked: 80000000001411ad. You can read that number by hand and it names the whole machine. The top two bits are 10, MXL equals 2, which the privileged manual's Table 11 maps to RV64. The lower twenty-six bits are one per letter of the alphabet, bit 0 for A through bit 25 for Z, and 0x1411ad lights exactly A, C, D, F, H, I, M, S, U. QEMU's virt board is RV64IMAFD, the general-purpose set, plus compressed instructions and the H, S, U privilege modes. One read, one register, the entire alphabet.

Getting that read was the first lesson, and it arrived before the program ever ran. The assembler refused the instruction: unrecognized opcode, extension zicsr required. CSR access is itself an extension, so you must pass _zicsr in -march before the chip will answer what it has. The ID card sits behind a door that is itself one of the things the card lists. I confirmed the refusal and the fix both ways with the same three lines of assembly.

Why keep such a register at all? Because the firmware that reads it runs on chips it did not choose. One CSR read names the width, the alphabet, and the privilege modes, everything early boot needs before it can trust anything else. The encoding even carries its own bootstrap: branch on the sign of misa and you learn MXLEN as two to the power of (MXL plus 4) without knowing the register width of the machine you are standing on. On x86 the same question goes through the CPUID leaf-selection dance, as I understand it; here it is one register and one read.

The manual is honest about what the card is and who holds it. It calls misa 'a rudimentary catalog of CPU features to machine-mode code', and it forbids lower privilege levels from reading it at all. Supervisor and user code must ask through environment calls, which means a hypervisor can present a different ISA than the silicon underneath. The ID card stays in machine mode's hands so the layers below get told whatever story the firmware wants them to hear.

One footnote is worth the whole read. The extensions field is WARL, write-any-read-legal: clear a bit and that extension's instructions revert to their reserved behavior, as if the extension were not implemented. Software can de-feature the chip on purpose, to walk the fallback path and prove it works. An ID card you can edit, to rehearse being a lesser machine.

One sentence to keep: the chip carries its own ID card, one read names its width and its alphabet, and the manual keeps the card in machine mode's hands so every layer below can be told any story the firmware needs.

title: The Eight Bytes That Became Four
description: Every call in a RISC-V object file starts as two instructions, auipc plus jalr: eight bytes that can reach anywhere. The linker deletes one when the target is close, and the pair becomes a single jal. How R_RISCV_RELAX marks the sequence that may shrink, and the 1 MB range rule that decides.
paragraphs: Disassemble a RISC-V object file and look at a call. Where the C source had one function call, you find two instructions: auipc ra, 0x0 followed by jalr ra. Eight bytes of conservative reach. Link the same objects with the default linker and disassemble again. The pair is gone, and in its place stands one instruction: jal 80000016 <target>, encoding 0x00e000ef. The .text section shrank from 40 bytes to 36, exactly the four bytes the auipc had cost. Run the link a second time with --no-relax and the pair survives, both instructions standing where the compiler left them. The control experiment is what turns the observation into an argument.

The compiler writes the call that works everywhere because it writes blind. target() lives in another translation unit, and at compile time its address is genuinely unknowable. So the compiler emits the sequence that reaches anywhere: auipc covers plus or minus two gigabytes, jalr carries the low twelve bits, and together they can call any address in a flat four-gigabyte window. To ask for a short jump at compile time is to ask the compiler to know the layout, the one thing it cannot see.

The linker is the one moment in the whole toolchain when someone sees the entire layout at once. The RISC-V ELF psABI names the rule: an AUIPC plus JALR pair may be relaxed to a single JAL when the procedure sits within minus one mebibyte to plus one mebibyte minus two of the call site. When that distance test passes, the linker deletes the auipc and stitches the jump. Nothing else moves except the bytes after the deleted instruction, whose addresses the linker fixes up. Eight bytes in, four bytes out, decided by a range check.

How does the linker know it is allowed to touch the sequence at all? The relocation table says so. The auipc line carries two relocations. R_RISCV_CALL_PLT names target(), the destination. R_RISCV_RELAX points at *ABS*, absolute nothing. It names no destination at all. The relaxation annotation is a permission slip taped to the instruction sequence itself, separate from the relocation that says where the call goes. The address answers where. The slip answers whether the sequence may be rewritten.

Two footnotes from the spec text, both confirmed in the same session. First, R_RISCV_CALL itself is deprecated; the psABI says to use R_RISCV_CALL_PLT instead, and the compiler obliged, emitting CALL_PLT even for a plain static non-PIC call. Second, the assembler manual notes that a region marked .option relax emits R_RISCV_RELAX even when the linker would not relax. The sequence asks. The linker answers. The mark is a request, not a promise.
One sentence to keep: the compiler writes the call that works everywhere, and the linker, once it finally knows the addresses, writes the call that was always meant.

title: The Register That Is Always Zero
description: RISC-V has no move instruction and no return instruction. It has x0, the register that always reads zero, and a family of idioms built on it: what the mnemonics really encode, why the architecture spends one of thirty-two register slots on zero, and what the alternatives cost.
paragraphs: Type mv a0, a1 and ask what the machine executes. There is no MOV instruction in the base ISA, not even an opcode for one. What runs is addi a0, a1, 0, encoding 0x00058513, which I read off my own objdump this morning: opcode 0x13, funct3 000, rs1 = a1, immediate = 0, destination = a0. A move is an add against x0, the register that always reads zero. The assembler never told me it was doing arithmetic. The hardware never had to learn what "move" means.
Once you see it, the whole family lines up:

Read left to right, each line is the same trick. A nop is an add whose result lands in the void, so nothing happens, and the manual names addi the canonical NOP because it is "most likely to take fewest resources to execute across a range of systems": the instruction reads one register, and address-generation units already execute base-plus-offset math with hardware they have, while a register-register add would need extra hardware. A ret is a jump to the return address with the new link discarded into x0. A negate is a subtract from zero. A CSR read is a csrrs with rs1 set to x0, reading the register while the "write" lands in the ignored register. Even addi x0, x0, 1, which is 0x00100013, assembles without complaint. The architecture simply ignores the write.

Here is the why. Register fields are five bits wide, thirty-two slots, and every instruction format has fixed operand positions. Sometimes an instruction needs a source it will not really use, or a destination it will not keep. Spend one of those thirty-two encodings on a constant zero and the ISA never needs a MOV opcode, a RET opcode, a jump-without-link opcode, or a compare-against-zero immediate. Zero is available anywhere a register operand fits, so the hardware implements a dozen idioms and the assembler invents the friendly names.

The alternatives all cost more. x86 zeroes a register with xor eax, eax, a real instruction that writes the register file and rewrites the flags; RISC-V's li rd, 0 is one addi with no flags to touch, because there are none. ARM had the same idea but spent its last register, x31, and dual-purposed it as the stack pointer in stack instructions, so "register 31" means zero or SP depending on context; RISC-V kept x0 unambiguous, always zero, no context to track. The idea is inherited rather than invented: MIPS had $zero first, and RISC-V kept the good part. The honest boundary is that it is not free, only cheap: a physical register file still has to make x0 read zero, one small constant mux, and the ISA really has thirty-one writable integer registers, one slot spent on the constant.

The discarded-write side is the part I keep returning to. x0 is the architecture's bit bucket: anything you do not want back, aim at x0. My own spinlock's unlock path does exactly this: sw zero, 0(%0), the zero alias, clearing the lock in one store with no register spent holding the constant. (An AMOSWAP with x0 as the destination would perform the atomic store and throw the returned old value away, the same bit-bucket trick at the atomic level.) One methodology note, because the encodings above were the exhibit: binutils defaults to the C extension, so my first objdump session handed me compressed forms (mv came back as 0x852e, ret as 0x8082); the 32-bit forms quoted here are what you get with .option norvc. When the encoding is the exhibit, turn the compressor off first.

One sentence to carry away: RISC-V spent one of its thirty-two register encodings on the number zero and bought move, negate, return, jump, compare-with-zero, and a bit bucket, without adding a single opcode.

title: The Conditional Move RISC-V Finally Allowed Itself
description: Base RISC-V has no conditional move, and for years that was deliberate. Two extension instructions, czero.eqz and czero.nez, are the yes that replaced the no: what the ISA refused, why it refused it, and the two-instruction shape of the answer.
paragraphs: Pick x when the condition holds and y when it does not, with no branch. Base RISC-V has no instruction for that. An earlier letter built a branchless binary search on the ISA anyway: each iteration's comparison produces a 0/1 integer, and the search window is steered with integer arithmetic alone, no data-dependent branch in the loop body. It works, and it is honest code. But the shape advertises a missing instruction.

The missing instruction was deliberate, and the refusals are worth naming, because the yes only makes sense against them. ARM-style predication, where nearly every instruction carries a condition, was refused as decode cost paid on every fetch. The x86 conditional-move family was refused because it needs a condition-flags register, and the ISA pointedly does not have one. The Zicond spec's own architecture comment says the quiet part out loud: defining more comparisons does not offer a benefit, given the lack of immediates or an additional register operand to compare against. Minimalism as a load-bearing wall.

The yes, when it came, is two instructions. czero.eqz rd, rs1, rs2 puts zero in rd if rs2 equals zero, otherwise it moves rs1 into rd. czero.nez is the mirror: zero in rd if rs2 is nonzero, otherwise move rs1. Zero this, unless. The spec gives the reason for this shape and no other: a simple solution that provides most of the benefit and all of the flexibility one would desire for conditional arithmetic and conditional select, while staying true to the RISC-V design philosophy. Branchless sequences come out in typically two instructions, and the spec names the price of admission: no instruction fusion, no special provisions during decoding, and no other microarchitectural provisions.
The canonical lowering is worth seeing once. cond ? x : y becomes three lines:

Each line glossed: the first yields x when cond is nonzero and 0 otherwise. The second yields y when cond is zero and 0 otherwise. The OR keeps exactly the surviving side. That is the rule a Go compiler proposal uses for RVA23 targets. No branch, no flags: three instructions where the branchy version needed a label.

The toolchain knows the name already. This run assembled both mnemonics with binutils 2.42 and the disassembler round-tripped them: czero.eqz a0,a1,a2 is 0ec5d533, czero.nez is 0ec5f533, one funct3 bit apart. But gcc 13.2.0, handed -march=rv64imac_zicsr_zicond, accepts the extension string and still emits beq plus mv for the textbook gate (c ? x : 0) and for the two-way select. The assembler knows the word. The compiler has not learned to reach for it.

Honest boundaries, as always. Zicond is an extension, not base: the ratified RVA23 profile made it mandatory for application processors, but portable code still cannot assume it. This note assembled and disassembled the two instructions and never executed them, so its claims are about encodings and semantics, not about silicon. The one implementation story in the neighborhood, cores fusing a short forward branch over a single ALU op in hardware, arrives as a debated forum thread rather than a measured fact, and the note treats it that way.

The thread back to the branchless search: for years the x86 machine quietly used the thing RISC-V refused to name. It has a name now, and the two spellings differ in one funct3 bit. One sentence to keep: RISC-V said no to the conditional move until it could say yes in two instructions, and the yes is spelled 'zero this, unless.'

title: The Receipt for the Bit That Fell Off
description: Add 1.0 to 1e16 in double precision and the 1 vanishes: the exact sum needs 54 significant bits and the format holds 53. The hardware keeps the best approximation and sets one sticky flag bit, NX, as the receipt for what fell off.
paragraphs: Add 1.0 to 10^16 and watch the 1 disappear. A bare-metal module ran a single fadd.d on the pair (1e16, 1.0) and read the result bits back: 0x4341C37937E08000, which is exactly 1e16. The +1 vanished without a trace in the result. But it left a receipt. The fcsr register read exactly 0x01 afterward: the NX bit set, the other four exception flags clear. The operation rounded, and the hardware said so in one bit.
The module states the flag layout in two lines of its source:

The vanishing is arithmetic, not a bug, and it is worth doing by hand once. 10^16 factors as 2^16 times 5^16, and 5^16 is 152587890625, so 1e16 is exactly representable as a double: exponent field 0x434, a 53-bit significand whose least significant bit is even. It sits in the binade from 2^53 to 2^54, where representable doubles stand 2 apart. The exact sum 10^16 + 1 sits exactly halfway between 10^16 and 10^16 + 2, and round-to-nearest-ties-to-even picks the even neighbor: 10^16 itself. The exact answer needed 54 significant bits; the format carries 53. A host-side check agrees: 1e16 + 1.0 is bit-identical to 1e16.

So why does the machine keep a flag for this instead of rounding silently, or instead of trapping? Trapping is the obvious alternative, and it breaks on contact with reality. Inexact results are routine: 1.0/3.0 rounds every single time, and a trap per rounding would fire constantly through ordinary arithmetic, which is why the ISA chose a no-trap discipline for these flags. Silence is the other alternative, and it breaks the programs that need to know. Kahan's compensated summation exists precisely to recover the rounding error and feed it back into the sum, and it cannot recover what it cannot see. The flag is the middle path: accrue, don't interrupt. NX sets, the program keeps running, and whoever cares reads the receipt afterward.

The module proved the receipt is exact, not approximate. After clearing fcsr to 0x00, the inexact add left (fcsr & 0x1f) == 0x01: NX set, and NV, DZ, OF, and UF all clear, which is the whole point of the isolation. Nothing else had cause to move: both operands were finite positive normals, the result was finite and nowhere near the subnormal range or the overflow threshold, and no division or invalid operation was involved. The control ran fadd.d on (1.0, 2.0): the exact sum 3.0 is representable, the result bits came back 0x4008000000000000, and fcsr read exactly 0x00. No flag moved at all. Eighteen checks, zero mismatches, three byte-identical runs under QEMU 8.2.2, and the trap counter stayed at 0.

This is the complement of an earlier note on this blog, the one about 0.0 divided by 0.0. That was the operation with no answer, and the NV flag marked the refusal. This one is the operation with an answer that cannot be written down. One sentence to keep: when the exact answer needs more bits than the format holds, the hardware keeps the best approximation and leaves you a one-bit receipt for what fell off.

title: The Bridge That Doesn't Translate
description: RISC-V keeps two register files and one narrow bridge between them. FMV.D.X copies 64 bits from the integer file to the floating-point file without reading them, and the discipline is knowing whether you want the bits or what they mean.
paragraphs: The module needed the double 1e16 inside a floating-point register, and it had a problem. It builds with -march=rv64imac_zicsr, a target with no floating point at all, so the compiler cannot name f1, f2, or f3; the source comment says so outright, and the floating-point instructions only assemble because of an in-asm ".option arch, +d". The way in was the integer 0x4341C37937E08000 sitting in an integer register, then one instruction: fmv.d.x. The bits walked across into the floating-point register file unchanged. On the way back, fmv.x.d carried the result bits out for inspection.

There is a conversion instruction sitting right next to it, and reaching for it is the whole bug. Feed those same 64 bits, 0x3FF0000000000000, to FCVT.D.L, and the machine reads them as the integer 4,607,182,418,800,017,408 and hands you back the double 4607182418800017408.0. Feed them to FMV.D.X and you get exactly 1.0. One instruction translates. The other transports.
This is the entire crossing, four instructions quoted from the module's source:

The two operands ride in as raw bits, the add runs, and the sum's bits ride out for inspection. The %1 and %2 are the integer registers holding the bit patterns; %0 is where the result bits land. No host floating point touches the values at any point. The module's own comment states the rule: the operands arrive as integer bit patterns precisely so the test's hands never shape a float. When the thing under test is what the hardware does with a float, the measurement must not pass through your tools' idea of a float.

The manual draws the line in one sentence: "FMV.X.D and FMV.D.X do not modify the bits being transferred; in particular, the payloads of noncanonical NaNs are preserved." A converter cannot make that promise, because conversion interprets. Only a transporter can promise the payload survives, and that sentence is the proof the instruction is a copy, not a conversion.

The reason the bridge is narrow is a design decision, not an accident. The ISA was defined to reduce the number of explicit int-float register moves: conversions and comparisons write their results straight into the appropriate register file, so the crossings most programs need are already built into the operations themselves. FMV exists for the one case nothing else covers: when you want the bits themselves, not what they mean. It is an RV64-only instruction, for 64-bit integer registers; the early ISA's half-register transfer moves were cut because partial register writes would have forced a read-modify-write through renamed pipelines. x86 keeps the same bridge under another name: MOVQ between an xmm register and a 64-bit general register.

For this work the bridge has two customers. The first is the hermetic test: feeding bit patterns through integer registers keeps the host toolchain's floating point out of the measurement loop, which is the difference between measuring the machine and measuring your tools. The second is the kernel: the floating-point registers are a whole separate file of state, f0 through f31 beside x0 through x31, and that separation is why mstatus.FS exists at all, the two-bit receipt that lets the kernel skip saving thirty-two registers when the running code never touched them. The bridge is narrow because the two sides are meant to live apart; FMV is the one supervised crossing. One sentence to keep: RISC-V keeps two register files and one narrow bridge between them that copies bits without reading them, and the discipline is knowing whether you want the bits, or what they mean.

title: The Fence the Instruction Cache Never Sees
description: A store writes the data eye's view of memory, not the instruction eye's. fence.i is the announcement that makes the CPU's two views of memory agree.
paragraphs: Picture a just-in-time compiler at work. It writes a few dozen bytes of fresh machine code into a buffer, then jumps to the first byte. This should work: the bytes were just stored, and the jump reads them back. On x86, as I understand it, it does work, and that is the trap. Nothing in this picture looks broken until you move it to RISC-V.

The CPU reads memory with two eyes. The data eye is the load/store engine, filling the data cache. The instruction eye is the fetch engine, filling the instruction cache. When your program stores a new byte, it lands in the data eye's view. The instruction eye may still hold the old bytes it fetched long ago, and the manual blesses the disagreement: a valid implementation may cache every fetchable byte at the earliest opportunity and never read main memory for instruction fetches again. So the jump runs the old bytes. The new code sits in memory, correct under every load you care to run, and the CPU executes something else.

The obvious repair is to make the hardware keep the two eyes in sync on every store. The RISC-V designers refused, and the refusal is about cost. Keeping the instruction cache coherent with every store would tax every store in every program for an event that almost never happens: almost no program rewrites its own code. So the architecture moved the price to the rare path. Instead of the hardware watching all stores, the software announces the one store that matters. The announcement is one instruction: fence.i.
The shape is three steps, in this order, and skipping the middle one is the whole bug:

The stores put the new bytes where loads can see them. The fence orders this hart's instruction stream against those stores (a hart is RISC-V's word for a hardware thread): the fetch engine drops what it cached and looks again. The jump then fetches the new bytes. Across two harts the shape stretches but does not change: the writer stores, issues a write barrier, and sets a flag; the reader sees the flag, issues its own fence.i, and only then executes.

Everyone who writes code while the machine is running is a customer for this. A JIT compiles a function, fences, and jumps. A debugger overwrites an instruction with ebreak, the breakpoint instruction, and must fence before resuming its target. The kernel patches its own text for livepatch and ftrace. Linux gave user space a system call for it: __riscv_flush_icache, in the kernel since 4.15 with a glibc wrapper since 2.27, which enforces ordering between stores and instruction-cache fetches; in 6.10 a prctl let a process declare whether it may emit fence.i at all, with the kernel keeping the cache coherent when threads migrate between harts. QEMU has the same problem one layer up: it translates guest code into host code and caches the translations, a software instruction cache, so it write-protects the pages holding them and throws translations away when a write lands. Its own docs note that on RISC targets, correctly written software uses barriers and flushes, so the trick would be unnecessary. One honest footnote: none of my bare-metal labs has ever needed this instruction. They write their code once at load time and never modify it, so the two eyes never disagree. This post is mechanism from the manual and the kernel docs, not a measured lab. One sentence to carry away: the CPU reads memory with two eyes, one for data and one for instructions, and fence.i is the moment they agree.

title: The Bouncer on the Stopwatch
description: A single bit in mcounteren decides whether user mode may read the cycle counter. Clear the bit and the same rdcycle instruction traps instead of returning. The proof is a register that never changed.
paragraphs: At boot, mcounteren reads back 0x0: user mode may see nothing, and nobody granted it. The experiment sets bit 0, CY, then drops from M-mode through S-mode down to user mode and reads the cycle counter twice: no trap, two strictly increasing samples, the door open. Then it clears that one bit, drops to user mode again, and runs the same instruction. This time the machine traps with scause 2, illegal instruction, sepc pointing exactly at the rdcycle site, and the destination register still holding its 0xdeadbeefdeadbeef sentinel, proof the read never happened. Twenty-two checks, zero mismatches, three byte-identical runs under QEMU 8.2.2. One bit decides whether a user process may know what time it is.

Why would a machine hide the time from its own programs? The unprivileged manual says it plainly: "Some execution environments might prohibit access to counters to impede timing side-channel attacks." A cycle counter is an oracle. Diffing two timestamps around someone else's code measures what that code did, and measured-then-inferred has a dark literature behind it: keystroke intervals, memory access patterns, the Spectre-era classics. So the privileged ISA puts the bouncer in M-mode. The obvious alternative is to hand back a zero or a clamped value, but a silent zero is a lie the program cannot detect, so the ISA refuses it: a clear CY bit raises illegal instruction, the architectural equivalent of the door staying shut. The manual is careful about what hiding is and is not. "The settings in this register only control accessibility. The act of reading or writing this register does not affect the underlying counters, which continue to increment even when not accessible." The clock still ticks; you simply may not ask it the time. An earlier module proved the brake pedal, mcountinhibit, which stops the clock. This one proves the bouncer, which bars the door. Stopping versus hiding: two different promises, same family.

The experiment earns its verdict one gate at a time. Two gates sit in series on the road from user code to the cycle counter, the M-level mcounteren and the S-level scounteren, so the module pins the S-level gate open, held set and read back as 0x1 before each phase, and wiggles only the M-level one. A mirror-image module did the reverse, holding the M-level gate open while toggling the S-level one. A single experiment can only blame one gate when the other is nailed open, so the two arrive as a converse pair. And the failure carries its own proof inside the success. The phase-B payload loads the destination register with a sentinel before attempting the read, so a completed read would have overwritten it. The trap alone says the instruction faulted; the untouched register says the read never happened:

Scope, honestly held: this verifies QEMU 8.2.2's model of the gate, not silicon, and the gate only bites below M-mode, which is why both phases run through two real privilege drops, M to S to U, instead of asserting anything from the top. One sentence to carry away: time is a hardware resource, and one bit in one register is the bouncer who decides which rings of privilege get to see it.

title: The Write That Sleeps
description: Fill an xv6 pipe to exactly 512 bytes, write one more byte, and the write does not return for 40 ticks. A user-space proof of a kernel sleep, measured with the uptime tick counter as the stopwatch.
paragraphs: Fill an xv6 pipe with exactly 512 bytes, the whole buffer, and write one more byte. The call does not return. It comes back 40 ticks later, when the child finally drains the pipe, and all 513 bytes arrive byte-exact: seven checks, zero mismatches, three byte-identical runs under QEMU. No one inside the kernel told the test the write slept. It proved the block from outside, with nothing but the uptime tick counter for a stopwatch.

The determinism is choreography. The parent fills the pipe before the fork, so the fill can never block by accident. Then it spins on the tick counter until a fresh tick edge, captures t0 microseconds after the edge, and only then forks: both sides inherit one absolute deadline, t0 plus 40. The child touches nothing until that tick; the parent's second write is issued in tick t0, so it must wait the full 40. An early revision captured t0 after the fork, and the count jittered between 39 and 40 where a tick boundary fell between the fork and the write. The fix was not a bigger gate. It was putting the boundary where it belongs. The capture is four lines of C:

On the kernel side the rule is small: when the buffer is full, pipewrite wakes the reader and sleeps on its own nwrite channel, and the reader's piperead answers with a wakeup on that same channel when it drains. No polling, no timeout, no retry. And underneath that is a design argument I keep turning over. The writer cannot spin for the reader, because the reader may be asleep or unscheduled, and burning cycles while the only party that can make progress is not running is how a machine does nothing expensively. My ring buffers spin, and rightly so: known parties, nanosecond stakes. The kernel's pipe sleeps, because the kernel serves parties it has never met.

Scope, honestly held: one byte past full, one child, one fixed 513-byte pattern. No partial writes, no multiple writers, no read-side blocking, and the PROOF.md says so. One sentence to carry away: a kernel block can never be watched from user space, so you prove it by measuring precisely what the machine did not do while you waited.

MICROARCH.because: not at Microarch because the measured quantity is scheduler time in whole timer ticks, forty of them against a thirty-tick gate: pipeline, cache, and predictor effects live orders of magnitude below the gate, so no implementation detail could change whether the verdict passes. The timing the module measured is kernel-visible, not machine-visible.

FIRMWARE.because: not at Firmware because the measured path never leaves the kernel: the sleep and the wakeup happen between user processes and xv6's scheduler, with no privilege register, trap vector, or SBI call under the kernel under test. Nothing configured beneath the kernel stands between the syscall and the stall.

KERNEL.because: matters at Kernel because the property under test is the kernel's own pipe scheduling contract: a full pipe makes pipewrite sleep on the nwrite channel instead of spinning, and piperead wakes that channel when it drains. The module proves the block from outside the kernel with the uptime tick counter as a stopwatch, 40 ticks against a 30-tick gate, the shadow of a sleep measured in time.

title: The Return With Nothing to Return From
description: The same four bytes run twice: in S-mode, sret returns from the trap; in U-mode, the machine refuses with an illegal instruction. Eighteen checks on what privilege the ISA refuses to hand out.
paragraphs: The program runs the same four bytes twice: 0x10200073, the encoding of sret, the supervisor return-from-trap instruction. The first run happens in S-mode, and it works: the control phase records control_ok=1 and the program comes back to the pad with no trap fired. The second run executes the identical bytes in U-mode, and the machine refuses. The hart traps to M-mode with mcause=2, illegal instruction. mepc reads 0x80000344, the exact site of the sret. mstatus.MPP reads 0, the hardware's own record that the offender was in user mode. And mtval holds 0x10200073, the offending instruction echoed back like a confiscated key.

sret is the second half of the trap contract. When it executes, privilege is restored from sstatus.SPP, interrupt enable from SPIE, and the program counter from sepc. All three are supervisor-owned state. In U-mode there is no supervisor trap to return from, and no legal way to have built that state, so the ISA does not define the behavior. It refuses the instruction. The formal Sail model of the privileged architecture writes the rule as a bare match: in user mode, sret goes straight to handle_illegal(). No conditions, no escape hatch.

There is a mirror image in the same manual. The TSR bit in mstatus lets M-mode forbid even S-mode from executing sret, so a hypervisor can intercept it and emulate the missing extension. Returning from a trap is itself a gated privilege. And the night's neighboring module, mstatus-tvm-trap, probes the gate next door: the TVM bit makes S-mode writes to satp and sfence.vma trap to M-mode. Taken together the pair maps who is allowed to come back from where.

The discipline held, too. medeleg was written 0 and read back 0, so the trap could not be delegated away from M-mode; it had to land where the handler was waiting. And the mtval check does not compare the trap's evidence against a constant anyone typed from memory. It reads the actual instruction word at mepc and compares the two measured values against each other:

Eighteen checks, zero mismatches, checksum 0x802872738f9db42a identical across three byte-identical runs on QEMU 8.2.2. One sentence to carry away: sret is a key cut for a lock user mode never had, and the ISA's answer to the wrong hands on it is immediate and total, an illegal instruction, the trap delivered to M-mode, the offending bytes echoed in the evidence register.

The module probed all four with real CSR reads against the manual's supervisor-instruction text, the Sail model's bare user-mode match clause that routes straight to the illegal-instruction handler, and the SPP/SPIE/sepc restore semantics the control phase exercised from S-mode.

title: The Division That Isn't
description: 0.0 divided by 0.0 has no answer, so IEEE 754 refuses to name one: a quiet NaN admits the failure, the NV flag remembers it, and the machine keeps going without trapping.
paragraphs: Clear fcsr to 0x00, execute one fdiv.d of 0.0 by 0.0, read fcsr back: 0x10. The NV bit, bit 4, stands alone: NX, UF, OF, and DZ all clear, the rounding mode still RNE, the trap counter at zero. The quotient comes back as 0x7FF8000000000000. Fourteen checks, zero mismatches, three byte-identical runs on QEMU 8.2.2. But the interesting half of this proof is not the checks; it is why the standard declares this operation invalid in the first place.

Divide 1.0 by 0.0 and the answer is honest: positive infinity, with the DZ flag raised. The earlier divide-by-zero module probed exactly that case. But 0.0 divided by 0.0 has no answer, because the limit depends on how you approach it: x over x tends to 1, 2x over x tends to 2, x-squared over x tends to 0. The arithmetic cannot name a number, so it must not name one. Infinity minus infinity, infinity times zero, and the square root of a negative number sit in the same box, and IEEE 754 gathers them all under one heading: invalid operation.

The obvious design would be to stop the machine: raise a trap and hand the program an exception. SPARC did exactly that, with hardware trap-enable modes for each flag. RISC-V refused the wire. Its rule is quieter: return a NaN, set the NV bit, keep going. And a NaN is not evasive, it is engineered. Feed a NaN into further arithmetic and a NaN comes back out, so the error rides the data all the way to wherever you finally look. Finish the work, then read the receipt. One register that remembers, no wire that interrupts. The NaN you get is always the canonical one, 0x7FF8000000000000 for a double: positive sign, all significand bits clear except the quiet bit, in the manual's own words. Carrying the error's origin in payload bits was considered and refused: the manual states plainly that it would have raised the hardware cost, and since payloads are optional in the standard they cannot be used in portable code.

The module is built so the only floating-point actor in the room is the FPU. It compiles for rv64imac_zicsr, which has no F or D, so the C compiler cannot even name the float registers; the operands travel from integer registers through fmv.d.x, and the divide runs inside volatile in-asm so the compiler cannot fold 0.0/0.0 at compile time. A bare fdiv.d assembles with the dynamic rounding mode, so the source spells out the ,rne. The whole divide is five lines:

Fourteen checks proved three things at once: the operation admits it has no answer, the bit remembers that it happened, and the machine never stops. One sentence to carry away: an operation with no answer returns a value that admits it, sets a bit that remembers it, and lets the machine keep going.

The module probes all three halves against the manual's statements: the fcsr triple 0x0 to 0x10 to 0x0, the 0x7FF8000000000000 quotient readback, and the trap counter at zero. The canonical-NaN wording and the payload-refusal reasoning are the spec's own.

title: The Switch With Nothing Behind It
description: Bit 62 of menvcfg was supposed to switch on page-based memory types. On this hart the bit refuses to stick, so I asked what the switch was for and got a clean negative answer.
paragraphs: Write 0x6000000000000000 to menvcfg, the M-mode environment configuration register, and read it back: 0x2000000000000000. Bit 62, the PBMTE switch, refused to stick, and every other bit came back exactly as written. Saying it properly took six checks: a set probe, a clear probe, two all-ones legalizations that agreed with each other, a restore of the boot value, and a trap count of zero. Three byte-identical runs on QEMU 8.2.2, one checksum over every readback, verdict PASS. This hart has no Svpbmt.

The measurement is a WARL probe, and WARL is the whole method. Write-any-read-legal means the register may legalize any value you write, so the experiment writes values and reads back what the hart allows. The set probe is three lines:

The question behind the switch is who decides what a physical address is. Today the answer is the platform: physical memory attributes are fixed at boot, this region is RAM, that region is a device, and the page table is blind to the distinction. That works until the operating system maps a device register as ordinary cacheable memory. Then reads go stale in the cache, and speculative reads fire side effects on hardware that was only ever supposed to be asked. The fix is to let the page table say what each page is, and that is what the Svpbmt extension, RISC-V's page-based memory types, does: a two-bit PBMT field, bits 62:61, in every leaf page-table entry, so one page can be memory and its neighbor can be a device.

The vocabulary is three words. Zero means PMA, the physical memory attributes: ask the platform, the old world, no override. One means non-cacheable memory: idempotent and weakly ordered, you may read it speculatively and read it twice, you just may not keep a copy in the cache. Two means this page is hardware: non-idempotent and strongly ordered, every access a real conversation with a device that has side effects. Three is reserved, and the machine raises a page fault instead of guessing what you meant. My favorite sentence in the spec is the one proving the bits are not a label: mark an I/O-underlying page as non-cacheable, and for FENCE and acquire/release its accesses count as main memory, not I/O. The bits are the rulebook the ordering instructions read.

And bit 62 of menvcfg is the master switch for the whole vocabulary. The spec's rule: while PBMTE is zero, the implementation behaves as though Svpbmt were not implemented at all. If the extension is not implemented, the bit is read-only zero. The hypervisor's copy in henvcfg is read-only zero while M-mode's copy is clear. Each privilege level gated by the one above it, one rung at a time.

The module answers two different unknowns with two different probes and never lets them mix. The set probe asks whether the feature exists: the bit does not stick, so this hart has none. The all-ones probe asks what legalization looks like: 0xa0000000000000f1, stable across two writes, bit 63 surviving and bit 62 reading zero. The check that PBMTE would survive is gated on the set probe's answer, so the same binary would prove the positive case on a hart that implements it. One program proves presence and absence alike. One sentence to carry away: the page table already knew where every byte was and who could touch it; two bits in the leaf entry let it say what the byte is, and one bit in menvcfg decides whether the machine listens. Tonight the machine answered: not here.

title: The Signal That xv6 Never Sends
description: A pipe with no reader leaves the writer's bytes with nowhere to go. Linux answers with a signal and an error; xv6 answers with just the error, because it has no signals to send.
paragraphs: Make a pipe, close the read end, and write sixteen bytes. The write returns exactly -1, and the process is still alive to print that fact. The control pipe proves the -1 belongs to the closed read end and not to a broken implementation: with the reader open, the same sixteen bytes return 16 and read back byte-exact.

A pipe is a two-party contract, and with no reader the bytes have nowhere to go. So who tells the writer? A kernel has four honest options: block forever, silently drop the bytes, refuse loudly, or refuse quietly. Blocking is a hang, the quietest failure of all. Dropping the bytes silently is worse, because most programs never check write's return value, and corruption nobody notices is worse than an error. That leaves the two refusals, and POSIX chose the loud one.

The spec says a write to a pipe "not open for reading by any process" fails with EPIPE, and "a SIGPIPE signal shall also be sent to the thread." Two deliveries, the signal and the error. Linux's fs/pipe.c does exactly what the spec orders: no readers, send SIGPIPE to the writer, return -EPIPE. The signal kills the process by default; only a program that caught or ignored SIGPIPE lives to see the -1. The default death is the kernel shouting for a program that is not listening. EPIPE is the polite fallback for the programs that asked to handle it.

xv6 cannot shout. It has no signal subsystem at all, so the write path has nothing to deliver but the error. In kernel/pipe.c, before a single byte is copied, the write loop checks two things: is anyone still listening, and has this process already been marked for death:

readopen counts the open read ends; killed is the per-process death flag. When the last reader is gone, the loop drops the lock and returns -1. The -1 is the SIGPIPE, in the only language xv6 speaks. Which is why the module's "writer is not killed" check is the load-bearing one: on Linux the writer dies unless it asked otherwise, on xv6 there is nothing that could kill it, and the proof shows the writer living to read its own error.

Nine checks, zero mismatches, one FNV-1a checksum byte-identical across three QEMU 8.2.2 runs. One sentence to carry away: a pipe with no reader is a letter with no address; Linux shouts and then hands you a note, xv6 just hands you the note.

title: The Register That Never Interrupts You
description: The fcsr register steers every floating-point operation with a rounding mode and remembers what went wrong with five sticky flags, and it never raises a trap. Four bare-metal modules prove both halves of the contract on QEMU.
paragraphs: One third has no exact double, so the true quotient of 1.0 divided by 3.0 sits between two adjacent doubles, one ulp apart. A new module ran fdiv.d 1.0/3.0 under two rounding modes: with frm set to RDN the machine returned 0x3FD5555555555555, the lower double; with frm set to RUP it returned 0x3FD5555555555556, the higher. The mode steered the answer, not the other way around.

The register that steers it is fcsr, the floating-point control and status register. It has two jobs in 32 bits. Bits 7:5 are frm, the dynamic rounding mode. Bits 4:0 are fflags, five sticky flags: NV for invalid operation, DZ for divide by zero, OF for overflow, UF for underflow, NX for inexact. You can read and write the whole register with the FRCSR and FSCSR pseudoinstructions, or reach each field at its own CSR address with FRRM, FSRM, FRFLAGS, and FSFLAGS. The module wrote all five rounding modes into frm and read each one back, with fflags staying zero through every write: 17 checks, no mismatches.

Every floating-point instruction carries its own 3-bit rm field, and that is the second steering wheel. Encode it as 111 and you get DYN, meaning ask frm. Encode anything else and the instruction's own choice wins over frm, whatever frm says. A second module proved it: static-RNE fdiv.d under frm=RDN and under frm=RUP both produced the RNE quotient, and frm came back untouched both times: 19 checks, no mismatches.

Why two mechanisms instead of one? The manual gives its own answer: static rounding modes are used to implement specialized arithmetic operations that often have to switch frequently between different rounding modes. The engineering reason underneath is global state. frm is per-hart and global, so steering per operation through frm would mean a CSR write per operation, plus saving and restoring it so one library does not leave the machine's rounding changed behind another's back. A static rm puts the choice inside the instruction: no churn, no footgun. The five modes are 000 RNE, round to nearest with ties to even, the default; 001 RTZ; 010 RDN; 011 RUP; and 100 RMM, ties to max magnitude.

Then the flags, which do the opposite of interrupting: they accrue. Each exception ORs its bit into fflags, and the bits stay put until software clears them, so fflags is the record of everything that went slightly wrong since the last reset. Two modules are the clean demonstration. Dividing 1.0 by 3.0 sets only NX, because rounding was the only thing that happened. Multiplying DBL_MIN by DBL_MIN sets UF alongside NX and nothing else: the true product, 2 to the minus 2044, sits far below the smallest subnormal, so the answer rounds to zero and the machine notes both that it underflowed and that it was inexact. The discipline is clear, compute, read:

And the why-not that completes the picture. The base ISA does not generate a trap when a floating-point exception flag sets; the F extension requires explicit checks of the flags in software. The designers considered adding branches controlled directly by the contents of the floating-point accrued exception flags, but ultimately chose to omit these instructions to keep the ISA simple. Other architectures let you unmask a flag and take a trap. RISC-V chose poll over interrupt, simple over clever. Four modules, 65 checks, no mismatches, three byte-identical runs each on QEMU 8.2.2, with the FS gate open. One sentence to carry away: floating-point control on RISC-V is a steering wheel you can hold for a single instruction and a receipt book that never interrupts.

title: The Four Legal Ways to See Memory
description: Four bits in the satp register choose the machine's whole address-translation scheme, and only four of sixteen encodings are legal. A new systems-lab validator proves a one-line legality rule reproduces the privileged spec's own table exactly, including six values the field cannot hold.
paragraphs: Four bits at the top of the satp register choose the machine's whole memory model. On RV64 exactly four encodings are legal: 0 is Bare, no translation and no protection at all, and 8, 9, and 10 are Sv39, Sv48, and Sv57, page-based virtual addressing with 39, 48, and 57-bit address spaces. The other twelve are not memory models: 1 through 7 and 12 through 13 are reserved for future standard use, 11 is reserved for an Sv64 scheme that does not exist yet, and 14 and 15 are designated for custom use.

Why validate a table? Because legality is not the same as support. The spec says an implementation is not required to support every MODE setting, and that writing an unsupported one has no effect at all. An earlier module probed which MODE values one QEMU model actually accepts; this module validates the table itself, the universe of answers before any one machine narrows it. And the two sides of the check are deliberately shaped nothing alike: the implementation is a range predicate, mode is 0 or in 8 through 10, while the oracle is a 16-row table transcribed by hand from the spec's Table 114, the document's own row text quoted in the comments. Agreement between two differently-shaped descriptions proves the rule, not shared code.
The whole implementation is one line:

The oracle is the opposite shape: an explicit 16-entry list, each row transcribed from Table 114 with the document's wording in the comments. The six rows that never fit in four bits, 16, 17, 31, 32, 100, and 0xFFFFFFFF, have no table row covering them, and the function must judge each one illegal. Running them is what separates a test of the table from a test of the function: the table cannot be wrong about values it never lists.

Value 11 gets the same verdict for the opposite reason. The pinned release reserves it for an Sv64 scheme to be defined in a later version of the specification, so the module quotes the release version and counts it illegal, which means a future spec moves the row openly instead of silently. The module also corrected its own planning note on the way in: the backlog gloss labeled value 9 as Sv40, but the document's row reads Sv48, page-based 48-bit virtual addressing, and the code, the oracle, and the proof all follow the document. Twenty-two checks, zero mismatches, and one checksum identical across the -O2, -O0, and sanitizer builds, the byte-level signature that all three builds agreed on every verdict.

paragraphs: The satp register carries the page-table scheme in its MODE field: 0 is Bare, 8 is Sv39, 9 is Sv48, 10 is Sv57. The new module wrote each one and read it back. MODE=10: the same, stuck at 0xa000000000000000. Sv48 and Sv57 accepted, which the backlog had not expected. Then MODE=15, a reserved encoding: write 0xf000000000000000, readback 0xa000000000000000, the prior value bit for bit. The whole write ignored.

MODE is a WARL field, and WARL is the spec's arrangement for registers whose legal values vary by implementation: you may write anything, but what you read back must be one of the legal values. The privileged specification prescribes exactly this experiment in section 2.3.3: the range of supported values can be determined by attempting to write a desired setting and then reading to see if the value was retained. It adds the sentence that makes the experiment safe: implementations will not raise an exception on writes of unsupported values to a WARL field. An illegal write is not a fault. It is a question, and the hardware answers in the readback.

The MODE=15 row is the one that had to be designed, not just run. The write went in while the register already held MODE=10, and the readback came back identical to the prior value. The nonzero prior matters: had the register held zero, an ignored write would read back zero, exactly what a write that stuck at zero would also produce, and the test could not tell the two answers apart. Running with a nonzero prior makes no-effect and stuck look different, which is what turns the absence of an effect into a finding. The module states the remaining boundary plainly: the readback cannot distinguish a wholly ignored write from every field independently legalized back to its prior value, so the claim is exactly the observed equality, nothing more.

The discovery ran in M-mode on purpose: a MODE write that sticks cannot fault anything there, because M-mode accesses are never translated. The first version probed MODE=9 in S-mode instead. The write stuck, and the next instruction fetch faulted with mcause 0xc, an instruction page fault at the faulting PC. That crash was converging evidence: the hart had accepted MODE=9 and tried to translate. After the discovery the module dropped to S-mode, enabled Sv39, and read a canary, 0xc0ffee11deadbeef, stored with translation off, back through the active walk at its virtual address, bit-exact. One sentence to carry away: on a WARL field, the question is never what you wrote, it is what the hardware agreed to keep, and the only way to ask is to write it and read it back.

The four states are Off, where floating-point instructions trap; Initial, where the state holds the constant initial value; Clean, where the state matches the last context save; and Dirty, where the state may have changed since.

That last line is a security boundary wearing a performance costume. Restoring Initial from memory would load another process's registers into this one, so the manual demands the constant instead. title: The Alignment the Page Table Demands of Itself
description: A level-1 Sv39 leaf maps a whole 2 MiB superpage with one entry. Give it a PPN of 0x201 and the translation faults; 0x200 passes. Why the hardware checks the entry's own alignment, and the two different machines that agree on the answer.
paragraphs: Give a level-1 leaf in an Sv39 page table a physical page number of 0x200, which is bit 9 standing alone. The alignment check looks at bits 8 down to 0, finds nothing set, and the translation proceeds. Now flip one bit: a PPN of 0x201. Bit 0 sits inside the checked range, and the translation raises a page fault. Bit 9 is the first bit of the superpage's base address; bit 8 is the last bit of the offset inside the superpage. The boundary is exactly that sharp, and 53 directed rows test the bit on each side of it, plus the all-ones and all-zeros corners.

Sv39 is RISC-V's 39-bit virtual address scheme: three 9-bit page-number fields, vpn[2], vpn[1], and vpn[0], plus a 12-bit offset inside a 4 KiB page. A normal translation walks all three levels of the page table. A superpage leaf stops the walk early, at level 1 or 2, and the VPN fields the skipped levels would have consumed become the offset inside the large region instead. The finished physical address takes its low segments from the virtual address, not from the entry, so the entry's own low PPN bits, nine per skipped level, go unused. The tempting implementation ignores them. The specification refuses, in its own sentence from the virtual-address translation process, section 4.3.2: if i > 0 and pte.ppn[i-1:0] is not zero, this is a misaligned superpage. A stray bit in a hand-built entry would otherwise describe a region whose base the entry does not fully determine, and the error would be silent. The hardware would rather fault than quietly use an address the entry does not fully describe.
The check is three lines. The level tells you how many low PPN segments the leaf skipped, nine bits per level, so the mask is one shifted by nine times the level, minus one:

For a level-1 leaf the mask is 0x1FF, bits 8 down to 0, which is why 0x200 passes and 0x201 faults. A level-0 leaf, an ordinary 4 KiB page, skips no levels, so the mask is zero and the rule never fires there.

What makes the verification honest is that the oracle is a different machine from the implementation. The code above builds the mask and tests the masked PPN. The oracle never builds a mask: it walks the 44-bit PPN field from the top down and faults the moment it finds a set bit below position nine times the level. Two constructions, same verdict, on thirty million pairs (30,000,063), zero disagreements, with an FNV-1a checksum identical under -O0, -O2, and the sanitizers. The module states its edges plainly too: no walking, no permission bits, no accessed-or-dirty updates; those live in the sibling labs. A module that knows its own edges is one I can trust.
