title: The Alarm That Will Not Leave Its Room
description: Pending is a fact, enable is a permission. The machine timer interrupt stays silent under a set pending bit until firmware opens its enable gate, and no mideleg write can hand it down to S-mode on this machine.
paragraphs: Light a fuse. On a bare-metal RISC-V machine running M-mode firmware, one 64-bit MMIO write of mtime + 5000 ticks lands in the CLINT's mtimecmp register for hart 0 at 0x02004000. The board's mtime runs at 10 MHz, so 5000 ticks is exactly 500 microseconds: a half-millisecond fuse, lit in software. Set mstatus.MIE, the master interrupt switch, but write zero to mie, the register with one enable bit per interrupt source. Poll mip, the pending register. Bit 7, MTIP, reads set: the CLINT, the core-local interruptor, lifted it when the running clock crossed the compare. Two million reads of the cycle counter roll by, a window in which an enabled interrupt would have fired within a handful of instructions, and the trap count stays zero. The fuse burned, the alarm rang, and the hart did not move. Then set bit 7 of mie, the MTIE enable. Exactly one trap fires. mcause reads 0x8000000000000007: the top bit says interrupt, the low bits say code 7, machine timer interrupt. The handler's first duty is to write mtimecmp to all ones, lifting the compare above the running clock so the alarm cannot refire. The second quiet window confirms it: the trap count stays exactly one. Three runs, byte-identical transcripts.

Why does the enable bit exist at all? The obvious machine needs only one: the pending bit says the alarm wants attention, so take it. The break is who writes what. The CLINT sets MTIP when the clock crosses the compare; no code writes that bit, the hardware raises it and only a disarm clears it. Firmware writes MTIE: that is the running code deciding, per source, whether it may be interrupted right now. Without the split, arming the timer would be taking it: the write that sets the deadline would guarantee a trap at the deadline, with no way to leave the alarm pending while the work in flight finishes. And the split is what makes the handler's discipline load-bearing rather than polite: clear the source first, then leave. With the gate still open and the source uncleared, the trap would refire the instant the handler returns. Phase C, the trap count staying exactly one after the all-ones write, is the test that the disarm actually disarmed.

Then the module's sibling asked the next question, and the answer is the better half of the story. If MTIP is just bit 7 of the pending register, can the alarm be handed down to S-mode, where a kernel would receive it? The backlog item assumed yes: set bit 7 of mideleg, the machine interrupt delegation register, and the timer interrupt should arrive in supervisor mode. The measurement said no. mideleg is a WARL register, write any value and read back a legal one, and on this machine bit 7 is read-only zero: writes of 0x0, 0x80, and 0x14c4 all read back 0x1444, the bit dropped every time, matching the earlier mideleg-warl module's published delegable mask. The module dropped the hart to S-mode anyway and armed the timer 500 ticks out. Exactly one trap, in M-mode, mcause 0x8000000000000007, zero S-mode arrivals. On QEMU 8.2.2's virt board, the machine timer interrupt has no other room to go to. The honest scope: this is the emulator's CSR model, not silicon; real silicon publishes its own delegable set.

The checks that carry the argument, verbatim from the two modules. The gate module runs twenty checks, zero failures; the routing module runs twenty, zero failures. Three runs of the gate module on QEMU 8.2.2 produced byte-identical transcripts, checksummed identically. That is what a tight test looks like: the expected outputs are small integers, a trap count of 0 or 1, a cause code, a register readback, so there is nowhere for nondeterminism to hide.

The module's notes hide a debugging gem worth stealing. The first routing build armed the timer 500 ticks out, 50 microseconds at the board's 10 MHz mtime, then printed its arm line before reading the armed value back. One UART line at 115200 baud takes about seven milliseconds, 139 timer expiries, so the readback measured history, not the arm. The fix reads the armed value immediately after the arm write, before any slow output. On bare metal, ordering a measurement around slow I/O is the experiment's design, not its plumbing. One sentence to carry away: a pending interrupt is a fact, an enabled interrupt is a permission, and some doors are not doors at all; measure which kind you are standing in front of before you try to walk through it.

description: Pending is a fact, enable is a decision. Two million silent cycles with the gate closed, then exactly one machine software interrupt when it opens.
paragraphs: Boot a bare-metal RISC-V machine in M-mode (machine mode, the most privileged; firmware runs here). Set mstatus.MIE, the master interrupt switch, and write zero to mie, the register with one enable bit per interrupt source. Now ring the bell: write 1 to the CLINT's msip register for hart 0. The CLINT, the core-local interruptor that raises software interrupts, lifts the MSIP bit, bit 3 of the pending register mip. Read mip: 0x8. Then wait. Two million reads of the cycle counter roll by, a window in which an enabled interrupt would have fired within a handful of instructions, and the trap count stays zero, mip still 0x8. The bell is ringing and the hart does not move. One more write: set bit 3 of mie, the MSIE enable. Exactly one trap fires. mcause reads 0x8000000000000003: the top bit says interrupt, the 3 says machine software interrupt. The handler clears the CLINT's msip, and the world goes quiet: the window after shows no re-delivery.

Why two bits for one interrupt? The obvious machine needs only one: the pending bit says the interrupt wants attention, so take it. The break is who writes what. The CLINT sets MSIP when someone writes its msip register: that is the outside world talking. Firmware writes MSIE: that is the hart deciding, per source, whether it may be interrupted right now. Without the split, a handler could never keep the timer interrupt armed while it services a software interrupt, because arming would be taking. And the split is what makes a level-triggered source safe: the pending bit stays set until the handler clears the source, so with the gate already open the trap would refire the instant the handler returns. The discipline that follows is to clear the source first, then leave. This is not a convention. A public bug report against an open-source RISC-V core's testbench described its MSIP stuck high from reset, so the first time firmware opened the gate the hart took a machine software interrupt nobody had rung for. Hardware logic, not habit.

The trap rule, from the privileged architecture's own text: interrupt i is taken when mstatus.MIE is set and both mie[i] and mip[i] are set. Three bits, one decision. mie is the enable half, written by the running code; mip is the pending half, written by the world, here by a 32-bit MMIO write to the CLINT at 0x02000000. The test checked the contract from both directions. With MIE set and mie at 0x0, a pending MSIP must never trap; setting mie bit 3 while MSIP is still pending must deliver the interrupt at the next instruction boundary. The machine timer was disarmed at startup, its compare register set to all ones, so the software interrupt was the only source that could ever fire; MIE stayed set for the whole run, so mie.MSIE was the only gating variable.

The four checks that carry the argument, verbatim from the module. Twenty checks in all, zero failures. Three runs on QEMU 8.2.2 produced byte-identical transcripts, checksummed identically. That is what a tight test looks like: the expected outputs are small integers, a trap count of 0 or 1, a cause code, a readback, so there is nowhere for nondeterminism to hide.

The same shape repeats one privilege level down, with the pen in a different hand. M-mode firmware owns mie.MSIE; a supervisor kernel cannot touch it. So its inter-processor interrupts arrive as supervisor software interrupts instead, raised through firmware's sbi_send_ipi. Linux's RISC-V interrupt handling dispatches software interrupts to handle_ipi(), the IPI handler. Two worlds, same pattern: someone else's firmware owns the enable bit, so your level gets the pending bit plus a polite ask. Two honest boundaries: this ran on QEMU 8.2.2's model of a hart, not on silicon, so it proves the contract as the emulator implements it; and the mepc readback in the test log is this exact binary's resume address, a measurement, not a claim about other builds. One sentence to carry away: an interrupt is not a request, it is a request plus a permission, and the permission is the half you get to write.

ISA.because: matters at ISA because the trap rule (an interrupt fires only when the global MIE, the per-source mie bit, and the per-source mip bit are all set) is the privileged architecture's own contract, and the module verified it with real register reads: mie at 0x0 held the hart silent under a pending MSIP, and mie at 0x8 delivered exactly one trap with mcause reading the machine-software-interrupt code.

MICROARCH.because: not at Microarch because the gate's verdict is a contract rule about register state, identical on every conforming implementation: no timing, pipeline, or cache behavior was measured, and none could change whether the trap fires.

FIRMWARE.because: matters at Firmware because mie.MSIE is writable only in M-mode, so the arming decision belongs to firmware: the module's phase-B write is the firmware action under test, and this gate sits in firmware's hands on every RISC-V system.

KERNEL.because: not at Kernel because a supervisor kernel cannot write mie.MSIE, so its behavior is invariant under this bit: its own enable is sstatus.SIE, and its inter-processor interrupts arrive as supervisor software interrupts through firmware's sbi_send_ipi regardless of the M-mode gate.

ALGORITHM.because: not at Algorithm because the enable/pending split is the architecture's privilege mechanism, not a portable technique: with no M-mode enable register the claim has nothing to mean, and nothing in the verified behavior travels to another machine.

title: The Bit That Reroutes a Trap
paragraphs: Run the same instruction twice. Boot a bare-metal RISC-V machine, drop from machine mode into supervisor mode, and execute ecall, the instruction that asks the layer above for a service. With the medeleg register at zero, the trap lands in the machine-mode handler: its cause register reads mcause = 9, the code for an environment call from supervisor mode. Write 0x200 to medeleg, which is bit 9 set, and execute the identical ecall again. This time the machine handler never fires. The supervisor-mode handler catches the trap instead, with scause = 9. Same instruction, two destinations, one bit of difference.

The bit exists because of who pays for every trap. The kernel runs in supervisor mode, and a system call is the most frequent request a machine fields: every file read, every byte on the terminal, every new process. Without delegation, each of those traps would rise to machine mode first, usually firmware, which would then have to forward it back down to the kernel that knows what to do with it. The obvious fix is a forwarder in firmware, but it sits on the hottest path in the system and would have to understand the kernel's business. Delegation removes the middleman: bit 9 of medeleg says supervisor environment calls belong to the supervisor, and the trap goes straight there. Trust, expressed as one bit.

The mechanism, step by step. RISC-V runs code in privilege modes: M-mode, machine mode, the most privileged, where firmware boots; and S-mode, supervisor mode, where an operating system kernel runs. A trap is the hardware interrupting whatever is running and jumping to a handler; each handler reads its mode's cause register, mcause or scause, to learn what happened. medeleg is an M-mode register with one bit per trap cause: when a bit is set, traps of that cause are delegated to S-mode instead of landing in M-mode. The test checks the contract from both sides. Phase one writes 0 to medeleg, reads back 0, and demands exactly one trap in the M-mode handler with mcause = 9 and the resume address mepc pointing at the captured ecall address. Phase two writes 0x200, reads back bit 9 set, and demands exactly one trap in the S-mode handler with scause = 9 and the supervisor's own resume address sepc at the same ecall.

The check that carries the argument reads like a receipt. Fourteen checks in all: the delegation readbacks, the exact trap counts per mode per phase, the cause codes, the resume addresses matching the captured ecall, the privilege records in mstatus and sstatus confirming arrival from supervisor mode, a cross-phase proof that no trap leaked into the wrong handler, and a quiet window where the counts were required not to move. Three runs on QEMU 8.2.2 produced byte-identical FNV-1a checksums over the verdict values. That is what a tight test looks like: the expected outputs are small integers, a trap count of 1 or 0, so there is nowhere for nondeterminism to hide.

Two honest boundaries. The module ran on QEMU's model of a hart, not on silicon, so it proves the contract as the emulator implements it: the specification's text, rendered in software. And the backlog item that ordered this test said the phase-one cause would be 0xb; the test asserts 0x9 instead, because the specification assigns 0xb to an environment call from M-mode and 9 to one from S-mode, and this ecall runs in S-mode. One sentence to carry away: the destination of a supervisor's system call is one bit in a register, and setting it is how the firmware gets out of the way.

ISA.because: matters at ISA because the bit itself is the machine contract: the privileged architecture defines medeleg, assigns cause 9 to a supervisor environment call, and says a set bit 9 routes that trap to S-mode. The module checked the contract's exact shape: identical ecall, two destinations, one bit.

MICROARCH.because: not at Microarch because the destination flip is a contract property, identical on every conforming implementation: no pipeline, cache, or branch-predictor behavior was measured or asserted, and none could change which handler the trap lands in.

FIRMWARE.because: matters at Firmware because firmware is the layer that holds the pen: medeleg is only writable in M-mode, so the decision to delegate is firmware policy, and the module's phase-two setup (write 0x200, read back bit 9 set) is the firmware action under test.

KERNEL.because: matters at Kernel because the delegated trap is the kernel's syscall path: with the bit set, a supervisor kernel fields its own environment calls directly instead of receiving them forwarded down from M-mode, which is the hot path the delegation exists to shorten.

ALGORITHM.because: not at Algorithm because the mechanism is the architecture's privilege rule, not a portable technique: a trap destination switch has no meaning on a machine without M-mode, S-mode, and a delegation register, and nothing in the verified behavior travels.

title: The Bit That Survives the Context Switch
paragraphs: Take virtual page number 0x12345, mapped with its page-table G bit set. Walk it under address-space IDs 1, 2, and 9: all three land on the same physical address, (0xABCDE shifted left by 12) plus the 0x678 offset, and every walk reports global equals 1. The address-space ID is never consulted. Now the contrast: the same virtual page number with G clear under ASID 1 lands on a page built from 0x11111, and under ASID 2 on a page built from 0x22222. Same number, different pages, because without the G bit the address-space name is part of the key.

Here is the cost it removes. The kernel is mapped at the same virtual addresses in every process, and every context switch loads a new satp register carrying a new ASID. A full TLB flush on every switch would throw away the kernel's translations too, and each one costs three page-table memory reads to rebuild, while the TLB holds only dozens to hundreds of entries. The alternatives are flushing everything every time or storing the kernel's mappings once per address space, the same entry wearing N name tags. The G bit says: this mapping exists in all address spaces, store it once, and when the fence names a single ASID, leave it alone.

The privileged specification says it plainer than I can. 'Global mappings were devised to reduce the cost of context switches.' And then the sentence that carries the whole contract: 'failing to mark a global mapping as global merely reduces performance, whereas marking a nonglobal mapping as global is an error.' G is a performance promise, not a correctness one, and lying in the wrong direction breaks isolation, because one process would start reaching another's pages through a shared cache entry. The entire rule fits in one line of the test bench, taken verbatim from the lookup it verified. One clause, two doors: global entries skip the ASID check entirely, non-global entries open only on an ID match.

The module proved the decision procedure, not silicon: 201,850 checks against an independently written spec table, zero mismatches, with the full result stream checksumming identically under -O0, -O2, and ASan plus UBSan. The rule held for 4K pages, 2M megapages, and 1G gigapages alike, and a branch entry's G bit was correctly ignored, because only the leaf's G decides. Two honest boundaries: the spec's own wording forks on whether a non-leaf G implies globality below it, so the lab tested the leaf-only reading and named the other as an open question. And the boundary I like best: xv6 sets no G bits and builds every satp with ASID 0, so the kernel I study never asks this question. One sentence to carry away: a translation is either named by its address space or it belongs to all of them, and one bit in the page table is the entire difference.

ISA.because: matters at ISA because the G bit is bit 5 of the Sv39 leaf page-table entry, defined by the privileged architecture, and the verified decision procedure is the specification's own contract: a global entry's translation applies without consulting the ASID, and an sfence.vma that names one ASID must leave global entries cached. The module's walks under ASIDs 1, 2, and 9 checked exactly that shape: global equals 1, the address-space ID never consulted.

MICROARCH.because: not at Microarch because the verified property is the contract's decision procedure, identical on every conforming implementation: the 196.216 ns per lookup figure is the host model's linear scan over 256 slots, an artifact of the model, and no hardware TLB, pipeline, or cache behavior was measured or asserted.

FIRMWARE.because: not at Firmware because the G contract runs between the hart and the page tables, and nothing in the verified behavior depends on firmware: marking mappings global and choosing address-space IDs is the kernel's work, and the property holds identically however the firmware beneath it behaves.

KERNEL.because: matters at Kernel because the kernel is the layer that names address spaces: it picks the ASIDs, decides whether its own mappings are marked global, and issues the address-space-scoped fences on context switch. The module's boundary check makes this concrete, because xv6 never sets a G bit and builds every satp with ASID 0, so its kernel never asks the question this bit answers.

ALGORITHM.because: not at Algorithm because the lookup predicate is not a portable mechanism: the claim has no meaning on a machine without a G bit in its page-table entries, and the module proved the architecture's rule as written, not a software technique that travels.

title: The Brake Pedal on the Stopwatch
paragraphs: Yesterday this blog measured the floor for reading the cycle counter. This note asks the opposite question: what happens when you stop it? One write of 0x1 to the mcountinhibit CSR, setting its CY bit, and one thousand back-to-back reads of mcycle came back identical, every one of them 0x0, a delta of exactly zero. One write of 0x0 to clear the bit, and the counter woke up: four samples, strictly increasing, with consecutive deltas in the tens of thousands of ticks. The brake pedal works.

But why would a CPU ship a brake pedal for its own stopwatch? The obvious move is to simply not read the counter, or to hide it with mcounteren, and skip the register. The privileged manual breaks that answer in one sentence: mcounteren decides only who may see the counters, and the counters keep incrementing even when nobody can read them. Hiding the stopwatch does not stop it. It still ticks, it still burns power, and any reading you take later is stale by the whole interval you skipped. mcountinhibit is the other promise, the one that actually halts the mechanism. The manual gives two reasons for the brake. The first is energy: a counter nobody is reading is heat and switching power for nothing, so M-mode firmware parks the ones it does not need. The second is atomic sampling, and this is the elegant one: one CSR stops every counter at once, so the cycle count and the instruction count can be read at leisure, knowing neither advanced in the gap between the reads. Without the brake, the two samples are taken a few instructions apart, and the pair lies about the same instant. RustSBI's performance-monitoring documentation says the quiet part out loud: from supervisor mode these counters can only be started, stopped, or configured through mcountinhibit.

The whole mechanism is one CSR write. Three lines, taken verbatim from the module. One call with the CY bit set freezes mcycle; one call with zero restarts it. Seven checks guard the behavior: the CY write reads back with the bit set, all one thousand freeze samples match the first, the clear reads back exact zero, the resume spin never trips its bound, the four resume samples strictly increase, the total resume delta is positive, and the trap count stays zero. Seven checks, zero mismatches, on QEMU 8.2.2.

Two honest boundaries. If two harts share one mcycle on a core, the CY bit is shared too, so one hart's brake pedal is visible from the other. And mtime, the wall-clock cousin of mcycle, cannot be inhibited at all, because it can be shared across cores and nobody owns the pedal. The QEMU note matters as well: on QEMU 8.2.2 the frozen counter reads back as 0x0, which is the model's choice, not the spec's demand. The spec requires only that it not increment, and the module asserts only that. That distinction is not academic, because this is exactly the corner where simulators have disagreed: Renode once shipped a bug where the inhibited counter advanced one more tick after the bit was set, filed as an issue with a reproducer, while Spike, QEMU, and RVVM all held still. The thousand-identical-reads test is precisely the test that catches that off-by-one, so the module is not only a demo of the gate, it is a conformance clause, and the model's answer is on the record. One sentence to carry away: a cycle counter is not a fact of nature, it is a peripheral with an enable bit, and the architecture gives M-mode both a curtain (mcounteren, which hides) and a brake (mcountinhibit, which stops), because seeing the time and stopping the clock are two different promises.

ISA.because: matters at ISA because the freeze is a contract clause from the privileged specification, section 3.1.12: with the CY bit of mcountinhibit set, mcycle must not increment, and the module's one thousand identical readbacks are the evidence the clause holds on QEMU 8.2.2.

MICROARCH.because: not at Microarch because the asserted property is the specification's non-increment demand, which every conforming implementation must satisfy identically: the simulators that returned anything else were buggy rather than differently valid, and QEMU's choice of readback value is observed but never asserted.

FIRMWARE.because: matters at Firmware because the brake pedal is M-mode's control to configure: supervisor software cannot write mcountinhibit, so parking the counters nobody reads and handing supervisor mode a start and stop interface, the role RustSBI's performance-monitoring documentation describes, is firmware work.

KERNEL.because: not at Kernel because the verdict was reached with the machine in M-mode throughout and no kernel loaded: whether the counter advances is decided by the CSR bit in hardware, so the property holds identically with or without a kernel running.

ALGORITHM.because: not at Algorithm because no software sequence can stop a hardware counter: the mechanism is the CSR gate itself, and the claim has no meaning on a machine without the bit.

title: The Page That Was Never There
paragraphs: Ask the operating system a question most programs never ask: how much memory can I actually have? The sbrkoom test asks it the blunt way: call sbrk(4096), the system call that moves the heap's break one page at a time, until the kernel says no. On a 128 megabyte QEMU machine the answer came back as a measured number: 32,468 pages, 132,988,928 bytes, about 126.8 megabytes. The break started at 0x4000 and stopped at 0x7ED8000, exactly 32,468 pages later, and a second sbrk(4096) still returned -1, so the ceiling is stable, not a hiccup.

Here is why the kernel cannot lie about this number. The test used the eager path, which is also the default: sbrk(n) calls sys_sbrk(n, SBRK_EAGER). The syscall calls growproc, growproc calls uvmalloc, and uvmalloc calls kalloc once per page, mapping each physical frame into the page table before the break moves. The -1 you finally see is kalloc finding its free list empty. No policy is consulted and no limit is configured anywhere; the pool of physical pages is literally exhausted. The machine holds 128 megabytes, the test drank 132,988,928 bytes of it, and the roughly 1.2 megabytes left over are the kernel, its page tables, and everything else alive at boot.

The obvious alternative is the one most programs live with: ask malloc and trust the number. On a stock Linux box that number can be fiction. The default overcommit mode is heuristic: the kernel approves the mapping and only discovers the shortage when you touch the pages, and then the OOM killer picks a victim and shoots it. The figure malloc hands you is a promise; the truth arrives later, as a dead process. My xv6 tree even ships the lazy twin of that design: sbrklazy moves the break without allocating a thing. The test pinned only the eager ceiling, and the eager one is the honest one: every page paid for in physical frames before the break moves, so the number it reports is measured, not promised.

The loop is the whole argument, six lines, taken verbatim from the test. p counts the pages the kernel agreed to, and the loop stops at the first -1, the kernel's only way of saying the free list is empty. Five checks guard the arithmetic: the refusal happened, the final break equals the starting break plus pages times 4096, a second request still fails, the heap end is page-aligned, and the size accounting is consistent. Five checks, zero mismatches, one checksum to recheck the numbers against. One sentence to carry away: a process's growth ceiling is not a configured limit but a measured fact, the exact point where the kernel's page pool runs dry, and in the eager design the kernel tells you the truth at that moment because it already paid for everything it gave you.

ISA.because: not at ISA because the claim is the kernel's growth ceiling, a count of drained page frames: the five checks would give the same verdict on any machine whose kernel refuses growth at its limit, so no machine-contract behavior is what the test proves

MICROARCH.because: not at MICROARCH because where the ceiling sits is set by the pool size and the allocator's arithmetic, not by the implementation behind the kernel: the test counts pages, and the count is indifferent to the core underneath

FIRMWARE.because: not at Firmware because the test runs in user space and the refusal originates in the kernel's page allocator: no machine-mode code or boot configuration decides the number the loop discovers

KERNEL.because: matters at Kernel because the growth ceiling is kernel memory management made measurable: sys_sbrk calls growproc, growproc calls uvmalloc, uvmalloc calls kalloc once per page, and the -1 the loop finally sees is kalloc's empty free list reported up the whole chain

ALGORITHM.because: matters at Algorithm because grow-until-refusal plus recheck is a portable capacity-finding protocol: grow while the allocator succeeds, confirm the boundary arithmetic, confirm the refusal is stable; it ports to any allocator with a hard failure signal

title: The Multiply With No Multiply
paragraphs: Base RISC-V, RV32I, has no multiply instruction. The mul instruction lives in the M extension, which is optional, and a core that skips M still has to multiply. The software that does it is what compilers emit and what this lab writes by hand. The obvious move is to write a * b and trust the compiler; on an M-less core the compiler has no multiply to emit, so it calls a library routine instead. The lab takes the harder road on purpose: it bans the * operator from the source entirely, then checks the compiled object to make sure the compiler did not smuggle one back in. The claim has to hold beneath the abstraction, so the check runs beneath the abstraction.

One you can check by hand. Take A = 0x00020003 and B = 0x00040005. Split each into 16-bit halves: a1 = 2, a0 = 3, b1 = 4, b0 = 5. Schoolbook multiplication is the grade-school kind: multiply every pair of digits and add the partial products at their positions. The expansion is A*B = a0*b0 + (a0*b1 + a1*b0)*2^16 + a1*b1*2^32. Modulo 2^32, the last term carries a factor of 2^32 and vanishes, and of the middle term only the low 16 bits survive the 2^16 scaling. So a0*b0 = 15, and the cross term is 3*4 + 2*5 = 22, times 65536 is 1,441,792. Add 15: 1,441,807, which is 0x16000F. Check it against the real multiply: 131,075 * 262,149 = 34,361,180,175, and mod 2^32 that is exactly 1,441,807. The shifts and adds agreed with the hardware multiply, without ever being one.

Each 16-by-16 partial product is exact in 32 bits, built the way lab/126 builds it: for each set bit i of one half, add the other half shifted left by i into a 32-bit accumulator. The lab's function is called mullo32, and the code is the insight here:

Four lines, taken verbatim from the module. p0, p1, p2 are the three partial products a0*b0, a0*b1, a1*b0. The masks keep only the low 16 bits of the cross terms, the shifts place them at bit 16, and adding them one at a time in unsigned arithmetic performs the inner mod 2^16 for free. The a1*b1 term is never computed at all: it would carry a factor of 2^32, so it cannot touch the low 32 bits of the answer.

The test oracle is the native expression (uint32_t)(a * b), deliberately a different computation from the schoolbook expansion, so agreement pins the identity instead of a shared bug. The source ban is checked two ways: a text search for * finds hits only in comment delimiters and prose, and the Makefile compiles the file alone at -O2 and fails the build unless the object contains zero multiply instructions. gcc 13.3.0 compiled the shift-add loops branchless, bit-test plus conditional move, and inlined them; the disassembly has no mul or imul anywhere. Lab/126 ran every one of the 4,294,967,296 pairs of 16-bit values, all 4.3 billion of them, exhaustive, zero mismatches, with one checksum identical across -O0, -O2, and the sanitizer build. Lab/128 ran 17,777,216 checks, 16.7 million exhaustive 24-bit values plus a million random 64-bit pairs, zero mismatches. Best of five at -O2: 47.232 nanoseconds per value, the timing honestly including the random-input step and the running accumulate, about the time light needs to cross a large room. The honest boundary: the module ran on the host toolchain, so what the 4.3 billion checks prove is that the shift-add construction returns exactly what the multiply instruction returns; the M-less core is why the construction matters, not where it was measured. One sentence to carry away: an instruction the base ISA never had, rebuilt from shifts and adds, and proved identical to the hardware multiply on 4.3 billion inputs without a single mismatch.

ISA.because: matters because whether a multiply instruction exists is an ISA contract question: base RV32I has no MUL, it lives in the optional M extension, and this lab is the software that contract demands on cores that skip M, proved to return exactly what the instruction returns

MICROARCH.because: not here because the verdicts are differential equalities that hold regardless of pipeline, cache, or predictor behavior: no microarchitectural fact can move any check, and the 47.232 ns figure is a timing ceiling, not a claim about any microarchitecture

FIRMWARE.because: not here because the module is ordinary userland C compiled by gcc and run as a process: no boot code, no PMP entry, no SBI call enters the computation, so nothing firmware does can move the result

KERNEL.because: not here because the multiply is a pure function of its two input values: whichever kernel schedules the process, the same inputs give the same product, so kernel behavior cannot move the verdict

ALGORITHM.because: matters because the schoolbook expansion on 16-bit halves, with the 2^32 term provably vanishing, is a pure computational mechanism: the masked-shifted combine performs the inner mod 2^16 in ordinary unsigned arithmetic, and the proof is exhaustive over all 4.3 billion input pairs

title: The Bit That Reads Execute-Only Pages
paragraphs: One page at virtual address 0x40000000, mapped execute-only: the flags read valid, executable, accessed, dirty, and no read bit. A page-table entry is the 64-bit word the memory-management unit reads on every access to decide what a virtual page maps to and what may be done with it; this entry may be executed but not read. Two phases, one load instruction. Phase A runs with MXR explicitly clear: the load raises exactly one trap, scause 0xd, the load page fault, with stval holding the faulting address and sepc pointing at the labeled load. t0 was poisoned to zero right before the load; after the handler advanced sepc past the instruction and returned, t0 was still zero. That is the part that makes it a proof rather than a story: the poison proves the load never completed. Phase B sets MXR with one csrs to sstatus: the identical load from the identical address returns the canary, 0xe4ec0d1edeadbeef, and the trap counter never moves past one. The only thing that changed between a fault and a success was one bit.

The natural objection: who marks code execute-only and then reads it? The privileged specification's own commentary answers. Section 4.1.1.6, checked in two copies of the manual this week: MXR was conceived for M-mode routines emulating missing hardware features, misaligned loads and stores being the example. A trap-and-emulate handler has to fetch the very instruction it is about to fake, and if the program's code pages are execute-only, the handler needs a read path that does not relax the page. If you own the pages, the obvious move is to mark them readable too. xv6 does exactly that: its vm.c maps kernel text with read and execute together, so the bit would change nothing there (checked in the tree this week). MXR earns its keep when the code is not yours to re-mark. It is the emulator's bit.
MXR is bit 19 of sstatus, and the whole mechanism is one CSR write: the hardware's load rule becomes readable or executable instead of readable. The code is the insight here:

Six lines, two of them the mechanism, taken verbatim from the module. The csrc closes the gate for phase A, the poison proves the load never completes, and the csrs opens it for phase B. The faulting load carries a global label, mxrs_fault_load, so the handler can check that sepc points exactly at the faulting ld, not merely nearby. One CSR instruction is the entire difference between a fault and a canary.

Thirty-one checks, zero mismatches, a checksum over the verdict values identical across three runs, and the raw UART outputs byte-identical. The honest boundaries, stated in the module itself: this verifies QEMU 8.2.2's model of the rule, not silicon; only the supervisor load path was measured, stores through X-only pages are untested, and the spec's rule touches loads only. One sentence to carry away: one bit in sstatus rewrites the load rule from readable to readable or executable, and the manual says it exists so an emulator can read the very instruction words it is about to fake.

ISA.because: matters because the gate is the privileged specification's own load rule in section 4.1.1.6: MXR=0 means loads need R, MXR=1 means loads need R or X, and the module measures exactly that contract on 31 checks with zero mismatches

MICROARCH.because: not here because the traps are synchronous and the run is single-hart on QEMU 8.2.2 TCG: no pipeline, cache, or predictor behavior enters any verdict, so microarchitectural variance cannot move the result

title: The Twelve Bits the Walk Never Touches
paragraphs: Take a physical page number, say 0x80000, and an offset, say 0xabc. The physical address is 0x80000abc: the page number shifted left by 12, ORed with the offset. A physical page number names which 4 KiB page holds your byte; the offset is the low 12 bits, which pick the byte inside that page. Everything this lab proves hangs on that split.

The part that keeps pulling me back is not the arithmetic, it is what the arithmetic refuses to do. A page-table walk never rewrites the low bits of your address. The privileged specification says it plainly in section 4.3.2: the page offset of the physical address equals the page offset of the virtual address. The tables decide which page your data lives on; the offset rides through the whole walk untouched.

It generalizes beautifully, and the invariant is the same at every scale. When the walk finds its leaf one level up, a 2 MiB megapage, the pass-through window grows: the upper page-number bits shift by 21 and the low 21 bits of the virtual address are copied verbatim, with the hardware faulting on a misaligned superpage if the low 9 bits of the page number are not zero. At two levels up, a 1 GiB page, the top bits shift by 30 and 30 bits of your address ride through, the low 18 required zero. Translation replaces the page number and copies everything below it untouched. The bigger the page, the more of your address the hardware trusts you with.
The code is the insight here:

Three lines. The shift moves page-number bit k to address bit k plus 12; the masks make the contract explicit, 44 bits for the page number, 12 for the offset, and anything above those widths is never read, so a stray high bit in a caller cannot leak into the address; the OR recombines two disjoint fields, so no carry can cross between them. Your xv6 walk() always descends to level 0, so every mapping it builds is exactly the 4 KiB case this formula covers.

The test is deliberately built nothing like the code it checks. The oracle never shifts a whole field: it walks destination bits 0 through 55 and sets each one individually from a single-bit extraction, so it shares no structure with the implementation and cannot share its bugs. 60,331,824 checks, roughly one for every second in almost two years, zero mismatches, and the checksum 235e187d99433244 identical across three builds. One conversion costs 4.275 nanoseconds, best observed, about the time light takes to cross four feet of a room. The honest boundary: the lab proves the 4 KiB case. The megapage forms above are verified against the spec text, not yet against a differential oracle, so they are the next rung, not a claimed proof.
One sentence to carry away: the page walk replaces the page number and copies everything below it untouched, and the bigger the page, the more of the address rides through.

title: The Gate With Three Locks
paragraphs: Take a page-table entry with R=1, W=1, X=0, U=0. Read the flags the way the hardware does: readable, writable, not executable, and owned by the supervisor, since U=0 marks a supervisor page. A page-table entry is the 64-bit word the memory-management unit reads on every access to decide what a virtual page maps to and what may be done with it. Now run a load instruction in supervisor mode against this page. The verdict comes from three questions asked in a fixed order. The load passes all three and proceeds. Run the same load from user mode and it dies at the second question.

The questions, in the order the specification's walk step applies them. First, the contradiction check: if W=1 and R=0, the access faults before any permission logic runs. Second, the privilege check: with the SUM bit clear (the lab states this boundary; SUM is the bit that would let the supervisor read user pages), a U=0 page is closed to user mode and a U=1 page is closed to supervisor mode. Third, the grant: a load needs R, a store needs W, an instruction fetch needs X. An entry with R=W=X=0 is not a leaf at all but a pointer to the next table level, so the grant gives it nothing, which agrees with the truth that it grants nothing.

The obvious design skips the first question and lets the grant logic sort it out: a page marked W=1, R=0 would simply fail loads and pass stores, writable-but-not-readable. The reason the specification bans the encoding instead is the invariant it protects: every writable page is also readable. If the contradiction could be written into a table, some piece of hardware would have to decide what a store to such a page means, and no two implementations would decide the same way. The fault keeps the contract free of contradictions, so no hardware ever has to interpret one.
The code is the insight here:

Three lines, and the placement is the point: this runs before the privilege check and before the grant switch, matching the order of the specification's walk step. The single condition is the whole invariant, writable implies readable, enforced at the gate rather than argued about later.

The proof runs every combination the table can express: 16 flag combinations times 3 access types times 2 privilege modes, 96 rows. That is the entire rulebook; there is no 97th row to miss. The oracle is built nothing like the implementation on purpose: the forbidden encodings as two explicit (r, w, x) patterns instead of the implication, the grant as a table instead of a switch, the privilege rule as its own predicate instead of early returns, so a bug hiding in one shape cannot hide in the other. Zero mismatches across all 96 rows, with the checksum efd3419afd2b56cb pinned across builds. One check costs 4.423 nanoseconds on this machine, a few billionths of a second, and a running kernel asks this question on nearly every memory access, millions of times a second, which is why the gate has to be cheap. The honest boundary, stated in the lab: this proves the leaf verdict only. Not the valid bit, not the accessed and dirty bits, not physical memory protection, not silicon. A proof that lists its own boundaries is the honest kind.

One sentence to carry away: a page-table entry's permission bits are a three-filter gate, contradiction first, privilege second, grant third, and the two forbidden encodings exist so that writable-but-not-readable can never be said out loud.

title: The Ten Fields in One Word
paragraphs: Take the word 0x20000007 and read it as a page-table entry. Bit 0 is set, so the entry is valid. Bit 1: readable. Bit 2: writable. Bits 3 through 9 are clear. Shift right by 10, mask to 44 ones, and the top field reads back 0x80000. A valid, readable, writable page at physical page 0x80000. Every page fault your kernel will ever handle starts with exactly this parsing step: xv6's walk() reads each level's entry to pull out the page number and check the permission bits. A misdecoded entry is a wrong mapping or a missed fault, so the parsing gets its own proof, small and focused, nothing else.

The obvious way to parse a fixed bit layout in C is a struct with bitfields, one named field per entry part, widths in the declaration. The honest reason not to is that C leaves bitfield layout implementation-defined. The compiler is free to pack the fields in an order you did not ask for, so the struct expresses a hope, not a contract. The lab decodes with shift-and-mask identities instead: one shift and one mask per field, every boundary explicit in the source. Shifting right by k moves bit k into position 0; masking with a run of ones keeps exactly the field width and clears everything above. The mechanism is portable to every ISA; only the boundaries come from the RISC-V contract.

The layout is the privileged specification's own: 44 bits of physical page number in bits 53:10, two bits reserved for supervisor software in 9:8, then the eight flags, dirty, accessed, global, user, execute, write, read, valid. The ten field masks are disjoint and cover bits 53:0 with no overlap and no gaps, so the fields partition the word, and shifting each field back to its position and ORing restores the entry exactly. That partition is the whole invariant: encode(decode(pte)) equals pte, and the test checks it on every one of the 4.3 billion cases.
The code is the insight here:

Three of the ten fields; the other seven follow the same identity. The flag order, valid up through user, matches xv6's kernel/riscv.h bit for bit, so the layout the lab checks is the layout a real kernel reads.

The best part is the promise about the bits the decoder never touches. Bits 63:54 are reserved for future use: decode never reads them, and encode always leaves them clear. That is checked, not assumed. Every directed edge value goes through twice, once bare and once with those top ten bits set, and the decoded fields must come out identical. 108 checks just for the promise that the future stays invisible.

The full count: 4,304,967,566 cases, more than 4.3 billion, zero mismatches. Every 32-bit word that exists, ten million fixed-seed 64-bit randoms, 162 directed edges, and the reserved-bits row. The oracle is deliberately built nothing like the implementation: one loop per field, each field assembled bit by bit through a pointer table, no helper code shared with the thing it tests. A second, independently written per-bit Python reference cross-checked 200,162 more values, also zero mismatches, and the checksum of every decoded output is e3c4316e414a6146. One honest caveat on speed: three timing runs on this noisy VM gave 25.782, 9.626, and 11.195 nanoseconds per decode, so the 9.626 number is the best observed, not a promise. One sentence to carry away: a page-table entry is a fixed bit contract from the privileged specification, and this test proved the decoder agrees with it on more than four billion cases without a single mismatch.

The piece checks agreement with that contract on 4,304,967,566 inputs with zero mismatches; the lab did not choose this layout, the specification did.

MICROARCH.because: the proof compares decoded field values against a per-field reference, a value operation on the input word: which bits sit at each position is fixed by the word itself, so no unmeasured pipeline, cache, or predictor behavior could move the result. The 9.626 ns figure is reported as a measurement, not part of the proof.

FIRMWARE.because: the decoder configures no trap vector, CSR, or privilege level; it treats the PTE layout as a bit-field specification to parse, the way one parses a file header. Firmware sets up page tables, it does not decode individual entries, so no firmware configuration stands between the input and the claim.

The verified property is the parsing step kernel virtual memory depends on; a misdecoded entry here is a wrong mapping or a missed fault in the kernel.

title: The Bit That Remembers Who Called
paragraphs: A bare-metal program ran the same trap twice and read the same answer both times. M-mode delegated supervisor ecalls to S-mode with medeleg bit 9, opened the whole address space with one PMP NAPOT entry, and dropped into an S-mode payload through sret. The payload issued two ecalls. Each trap landed in the S-mode handler, which read three values: SPP = 1, scause = 9, sepc = 0x800002a8, identical on both traps. The word sitting at that address was 0x73, the ecall instruction itself.

SPP is bit 8 of sstatus, and the hardware writes it at the instant of the trap: the privilege mode the hart was in just before the trap. In the same breath it copies the old interrupt-enable bit into SPIE and clears SIE, so no interrupt can re-enter the handler mid-stream. When the handler executes sret, the reverse happens: the privilege mode is restored from SPP, SIE from SPIE, then SPIE is set to 1, SPP cleared to 0, and the hart resumes at sepc. Push on trap, pop on sret. The trap path has a call stack exactly one frame deep, and the hardware maintains it.

Why does the hardware keep this record? Because one S-mode handler fields traps from two very different callers, and nothing else remembers which one called. The xv6 source tree checks it the way the hardware means it to be checked. In usertrap(), near the top of the function: if ((r_sstatus() & SSTATUS_SPP) != 0) panic("usertrap: not from user mode"). In kerneltrap(): if ((sstatus & SSTATUS_SPP) == 0) panic("kerneltrap: not from supervisor mode"). And usertrapret() deliberately clears SPP to 0, with the comment "clear SPP to 0 for user mode", before sret returns to the process. The hardware record is the only one that cannot be forged or miscomputed, because it is written at the exact instant of the trap. Without it the handler would have to infer the caller from sepc or saved state, and a kernel should not guess about who it was talking to.

One wrinkle, and it is the honest kind: one bit is one frame. Every trap overwrites SPP, so a trap taken inside the handler destroys the first record. The module's handler therefore reads sstatus before it dispatches on scause, copying the bit into a sticky per-trap slot, straight from ssp_trap.S:

The handler's trap entry reads sstatus before it dispatches on scause, copying bit 8 into a sticky per-trap slot in three instructions: read the CSR, shift right by 8, AND with 1. The code is the insight here; the snippet is on the page.

The record only survives if the handler keeps its own copy, the same discipline as saving callee-saved registers. The M-mode sibling works the same way one level up, except MPP holds two bits because M-mode traps can arrive from three levels: user, supervisor, or machine, with MPIE and MIE mirroring SPIE and SIE around mret. The checking, because that is the whole point: 11 checks, zero failures, and the three QEMU runs byte-identical, the same checksum 0x81dc6b1b81f94783 over the recorded values every time. One honest boundary from the proof file: this measures QEMU's model of the privileged contract, not silicon, and only the synchronous S-mode ecall path; interrupts, page faults, and traps from user mode are separate measurements. One sentence to carry away: every trap is a function call performed by hardware, and SPP is the return address it writes down for you.

MICROARCH.because: no pipeline, cache, or predictor behavior is measured or claimed; the traps are synchronous and the module times nothing.

FIRMWARE.because: the M-mode half of the module is firmware work: it sets medeleg bit 9, opens the address space with one PMP NAPOT entry, and srets into S-mode, and that setup makes the S-mode measurement possible.

KERNEL.because: the S-mode handler is the kernel's trap entry, and the bit is load-bearing for real kernels: xv6's usertrap and kerneltrap panic when SPP contradicts the expected caller.

title: The Four Bytes the Trap Handler Skips
paragraphs: A trap fires, say a load from an unmapped address. The hardware writes the faulting instruction's address into the mepc register and jumps to your handler. When the handler returns, the CPU resumes at whatever mepc points to. If the handler changed nothing, the CPU re-runs the same bad load, traps again, and you have an infinite loop. So the handler's most basic job is to move mepc past the dead instruction before returning.

How far past? RISC-V instructions arrive in 16-bit parcels, and the length hides in the lowest two bits of the first parcel: anything but 11 there is a 16-bit compressed instruction, and 11 starts the longer forms. A handler that blindly adds 4 will land in the middle of an instruction whenever the faulting one was compressed, and the CPU will try to execute half an instruction.

This module pins the fault site to exactly 4 bytes, twice over. First it assembles the faulting load under .option norvc, which tells the assembler to emit no compressed instructions in that region. Then it refuses to trust that promise alone: it captures the address on both sides of the faulting load with in-assembly numeric local labels, la t0, 1f before and 1: after, and the test asserts at runtime that the two addresses differ by exactly 4.

Why in-assembly labels instead of a C labels-as-values label? A C label only stays where the programmer put it if a computed goto can reach it. With no computed goto in range, -O2 is free to merge blocks and move the label, and the captured address follows the label to its new home. An assembler numeric label is resolved by the assembler exactly where written. That is the whole reason, and the construction is trustworthy because of it.

The test then proves the skip happened exactly once: the trap counter reads exactly 1, since a re-trap would have made it 2; the 0xdeadbeefdeadbeef marker still sits at its address, since a skip of 8 would have sailed over it; mcause reads 5 for a load access fault with the bad address in mtval; the instruction word at the fault address reads 0x0005a503, the intended lw; and the destination register still holds its pre-fault sentinel, proving the faulting load never committed. Three QEMU runs, byte-identical.

One honest boundary. The xv6 kernel gets away with mepc += 4 after an ecall only because ecall has no compressed form. This module is the general case: prove the instruction's length first, then skip it. And the verification is against QEMU's M-mode model, which is faithful, but it is still a model, not silicon. In one sentence: a trap handler that skips must know the instruction's length, and the only length worth trusting is one measured at runtime from both sides of the fault.
